By the same author, On the Incomprehensible, delivered in the bishop's absence, against the Anomoeans. First homily.

1. What is this? The shepherd is not here, and yet the sheep stand in perfect order. This is the shepherd's achievement: his flock shows complete devotion not only when he is present but when he is away. With dumb animals, when the one who leads them out to pasture is absent, the sheep have to stay inside their pens, or else, if they slip out of the fold without their shepherd, they wander far astray. Here nothing of the kind has happened. Even without your shepherd you have come to your usual pastures in perfect order. Or rather, the shepherd is here too: if not in the flesh, then in his affection; if not by his bodily presence, then in the good order of his flock. That is why I admire him and call him blessed all the more, because he has been able to instil such zeal in you. We admire a general most of all when his troops keep good order even in his absence. Paul looked for this in his disciples too, when he said: "Therefore, my brothers, as you have always obeyed, not only as in my presence but much more in my absence." Why "much more in my absence"? Because while the shepherd is present, even if a wolf attacks the flock, it is easily driven away from the sheep. When he is absent, the flock is bound to be in greater danger, since there is no one to wall them in. Besides, when he is present he shares with them the rewards of their zeal; when he is absent, he lets their achievement be seen as theirs alone. Your teacher too said these things and talks with you now, and wherever he may be, he pictures you and your assembly at this moment. He does not see the people who are there with him, in his presence, as clearly as he now sees you who are absent. I know his love: seething, on fire, warm and unrestrained. He has it rooted deep in his mind, and he tends it with great zeal. For he knows clearly that the chief point [?]

[?] For without this we shall utterly lose even our being human. "Fear God," it says, "and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of man." So if this is what it is to be human, to fear God, and the fear of God comes from knowledge, and knowledge is going to be abolished, as Paul says, then we shall perish entirely once there is no knowledge. Everything that makes us what we are will be gone, and we shall be no better off than the brute beasts, but much worse. For this is where we surpass them, since in every bodily quality they beat us by a wide margin. What, then, does Paul mean, and what is he speaking about, when he says, "Knowledge will be abolished"? He does not say this of knowledge as a whole but of partial knowledge. By "abolition" he means progress toward something better, so that partial knowledge, once abolished, is no longer partial but complete. When a child's age is abolished, his substance does not vanish; his age increases and he grows into a mature man. The same happens with knowledge. This small knowledge, he says, will no longer be small, because in time it will become great. That is what "is abolished" means, and he made this clearer to us in what follows. So that when you hear "is abolished" you would not think it means complete destruction, but a kind of growth and advance toward the better, after saying "is abolished" he went on: "For we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, then what is in part will be abolished." That is, it will no longer be in part but complete. So what is incomplete in it is abolished, so that it is no longer incomplete but complete. This abolition, then, is a fulfilment and an advance to something greater.

3. And notice Paul's wisdom. He did not say, "We know a part," but, "We know in part," showing that we hold only a part of a part. Perhaps you want to hear how large a part we hold and how much is left, and whether we hold the greater share or the lesser. Then, so that you may learn that you hold the lesser share, and not simply the lesser but, as one might say, a hundredth or a ten-thousandth, listen to what follows. Or rather, before I read you the apostle's words, I will give you an illustration that can show you, so far as an illustration can, how much is left and how much we now hold. How great, then, is the difference between the knowledge that will be given to us and the knowledge we have now? As great as the difference between a grown man and a nursing infant. That is how far the future knowledge surpasses the present. And that this is true, and that the one is so much greater than the other, let Paul himself tell us again. Having said, "We know in part," and wanting to show how small a part, and that what we hold now is the very least, he went on: "When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child; but when I became a man, I put an end to childish things." He compares present knowledge to that of a child, and future knowledge to that of a grown man. And he did not say, "When" [?] [A manuscript: "calling it progress, so that partial knowledge, once abolished, is no longer partial." [?] "to present, so far as an illustration allows, the very thing we are asking about, and to show how much."]

That is how great an evil it is not to stay within the boundaries God set for us from the beginning. So Adam too, in hope of greater honour, fell even from the honour he had. The same thing happens with lovers of money: many, craving more, have often lost even what they had. So too these people, expecting to possess everything here, have fallen even from the part. That is why I urge you to flee their madness. It is the height of madness to insist on knowing what God is in his essence. And to show you that this is the height of madness, I will make it clear to you from the prophets. The prophets are plainly ignorant not only of what he is in his essence; they are even at a loss about his wisdom and how great it is. Yet his essence does not come from his wisdom; his wisdom comes from his essence. If the prophets cannot grasp even his wisdom precisely, what madness it would be to think one could subject his very essence to one's own reasonings! Let us hear, then, what the prophet says about it: "Your knowledge is too wonderful for me." Or rather, let us take the passage from further back: "I will give thanks to you, for you are fearfully wonderful." What does "fearfully" mean? We admire many things now, but without fear, such as the beauty of columns, painted figures, the bloom of bodies. We also admire the vastness of the sea and its boundless depth, but with fear, when we peer down into the deep. In the same way the prophet, peering down into the boundless, gaping ocean of God's wisdom, grew dizzy, and drew back in fearful wonder, crying out: "I will give thanks to you, for you are fearfully wonderful; your works are wonderful." And again: "Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is too strong, I cannot attain to it." See the gratitude of a servant. "I thank you," he says, "for this, that I have a Master who is beyond comprehension." He is not speaking here of the essence; he passed over that as something everyone agrees is incomprehensible. He says this about God's being present everywhere, showing that he does not know even this: how God is present everywhere. To see that this is what he means, listen to what follows: "If I go up to heaven, you are there; if I go down to Hades, you are present." Do you see how he is present everywhere? Yet the prophet does not know how; he grows dizzy, is at a loss, and is afraid merely at taking the thought into his mind. Is it not, then, the utmost folly for people so far removed from his grace to pry into the very essence of God? And this is the same prophet who says, "You have shown me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom." Yet though he learned the uncertain and hidden things of God's wisdom, he says of that wisdom itself that it is boundless and incomprehensible. "For great is the Lord," he says, "and great is his strength, and of his understanding there is no number," that is, there is no comprehending it. What are you saying? His wisdom is incomprehensible to the prophet, and his essence is comprehensible to us? Is this not plain madness? His greatness has no limit, and you circumscribe his essence?

5. Isaiah too was reflecting on these things when he said, "Who will declare his generation?" He did not say, "Who declares," but [?]

[Two manuscripts: "For I think it the height of madness to insist." Morel and some manuscripts: "painted figures"; others: "of walls, painting." A little later some manuscripts: "the expanse of the sea" [?]. Some manuscripts: "and is utterly at a loss and is merely troubled." One has "strikes together" [?].]

[?] He knows that God exists, but what he is in his essence he does not know. He knows that God is wise, but how wise he is he does not know. He is not ignorant that God is great, but how great, or what his greatness is, he does not know. He knows that God is present everywhere, but how, he does not know. He is not ignorant that God provides for all things and holds them together and governs them precisely, but the manner in which he does these things he does not know. That is why Paul said, "We know in part and we prophesy in part."

6. But, if you will, let us leave Paul and the prophets and go up to heaven, in case there are some there who know what God is in his essence. Of course, even if some are found who know, that has nothing to do with us, for the gap between angels and humans is great. Still, so that you may learn all the more surely that no created power there knows this either, let us listen to the angels. What then? Do they discuss this essence there and investigate it among themselves? Not at all. What do they do? They glorify, they worship, they ceaselessly send up their hymns of victory and their mystical songs with great awe. Some say, "Glory to God in the highest"; the seraphim say, "Holy, holy, holy," and turn their eyes away, unable to bear even God's condescension; the cherubim say, "Blessed be his glory from his place." Not that there is a place around God, perish the thought! It is as we would say, speaking in human terms, "wherever he is," or "however he is," if even this is safe to say of God; for we have a human tongue. Do you see how great the fear is above, how great the contempt below? They glorify; these people meddle. They praise; these people pry. They hide their faces; these people insist on staring shamelessly at the glory that cannot be described. Who would not groan, who would not lament them for their derangement and this extreme folly?

I wanted to carry the discussion further, but since this is the first time I have entered these contests, I think it better for you that we be content for now with what has been said, so that the mass of what is still to be said does not come rushing in and sweep away the memory of this as well. In any case, if God permits, we shall work at this subject at length from now on. For I have long been in labour to speak these words to you. I kept intending to, and kept putting it off, because I saw many of those sick with this disease listening to us with pleasure. Not wanting to scare off the game, I held my tongue from these contests for the time being, so that once I had firmly caught them I might then strip for the fight. But since, by the grace of God, I have heard them calling on me and pressing me to enter these contests, I have now stripped with confidence and taken up the weapons that "pull down reasonings and every height raised up against the knowledge of God." I have taken up these weapons not to strike down my opponents but to raise up those who have fallen. Such is the power of these weapons: they know how to strike those who are contentious, but those who listen with good will [?] with great [?] with safety [?]

[Variants: "and to persuade them to be moderate" [?]; "knows, nor any other created thing"; "[they] praise" [?] — but here one should read "they pry" [?]. Some manuscripts: "to men." [?] "For what thanks," he says, "is it to you if" [?]]

[?] show me the praise in your deeds. A wrestler trains in the gymnasium so that in the contests he may show the benefit of that training. So you too, when anger comes upon you, show the profit you have gained from listening here, and say these words over and over: "If I have spoken wrongly, testify to the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?" Write this on your mind. That is why I keep reminding you of these words: so that everything said may be planted in your soul, and the memory, and the benefit that comes from the memory, may remain indelible. For if we have these words written across the breadth of our mind [?]

[Savile and some others: "and to persuade them to be moderate."]

By the same author, who had spoken against the Anomoeans many days before, then against the Jews, then fell silent because bishops were present and many commemorations of martyrs took place, and now speaks again against the Anomoeans on the incomprehensible. Second homily.

1. Come, then, let us strip again for the contest against the unbelieving Anomoeans. If they are annoyed at being called unbelievers, let them flee the thing, and I will hide the name. Let them give up their unbelieving way of thinking, and I will give up the shameful title. But if they themselves are not ashamed to dishonour the faith by their deeds and disgrace themselves, why are they angry with us for charging them in words with what they themselves display in deeds?

The other day, as you remember, when we entered the arena of these discussions and took up these same contests, the struggles against the Jews immediately took their place, and it was not safe to neglect our own members who had fallen sick. Discourses against the Anomoeans are always in season. But at that time, unless we had acted first and snatched those of our brothers who were weak and sick with Jewish practices straight out of the Jewish fire, our exhortation would have done no good afterwards, since their sin during the fast would already have been committed. After those struggles against them came in turn the presence of many spiritual fathers who had arrived here from many places. Even then it was not the right time for us to extend our own discourse, when all of them were flowing like rivers into this spiritual sea. And after their departure came commemorations of martyrs, one after another in close succession, and it was not right to disregard the blessing of those champions. I say and recount this so that you will not think it was from some reluctance or laziness that we put off our contests against those people. Now, then, since we have been released from the battle against the Jews, and the fathers have returned to their own homelands, and we have enjoyed the martyrs' blessing in full, come, let us at last relieve the long labour pains of your listening. For I know well that each of you is in labour to hear discourses on these matters no less than I am to speak them. The reason is that our city has loved Christ from the beginning, and you have received this as an ancestral inheritance: never to stand by and watch the doctrines of true religion being corrupted. How is this clear? Some people once came down from Judea, in the time of our ancestors [?]

[Others: "and driving away."]

[?] entrusted with the protection of the whole people of God. This Zechariah went into the holy of holies, into the innermost sanctuary itself, which at that time he alone of all men was permitted to see. (And consider how he was a counterweight to the whole multitude, so that he offered prayers to God on behalf of all the people and made the Master merciful to his servants. Do you see the greatness of his boldness of speech? He was like a mediator between God and men.) There he saw an angel standing inside, and since the sight struck the man with terror, the angel said, "Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard, and see, you will bear a son." What kind of connection is this? He was pleading for the people, praying for their sins, asking pardon for his fellow servants, and the angel says, "Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been heard," and gives as proof that it was heard the fact that a son, John, would be born to him? And quite reasonably. Since he was pleading for the sins of the people, and he was going to beget a son who would cry out, "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," the angel reasonably says, "Your prayer has been heard, and you will bear a son." What, then, did Zechariah do? The point we are looking into is this: prying into the manner in which divine oracles are fulfilled is unpardonable; their pronouncements must be received in faith. He looked at his age, at his grey hair, at his weakened body; he looked at his wife's barrenness, and he disbelieved, and sought to learn the manner, and said, "How shall I know this?" "How," he means, "will this be? Look, I am old and grey, and my wife is barren and advanced in years. The time of life is past, nature is useless. How does what was promised make sense? I who sow am weak; the field is barren." Does he not seem to some to deserve pardon, looking for the natural course of things and appearing to say something reasonable? But God did not think he deserved it, and quite rightly. When God pronounces, one must not stir up reasonings, nor put forward the natural course of things, nor the necessity of nature, nor anything else of the kind. The power of his pronouncement is above all these things and is cut short by no obstacle. What are you doing, man? God makes a promise, and you take refuge in your age and put forward old age? Is old age stronger than God's promise? Is nature mightier than the Creator of nature? Do you not know that his works are mightier than words? His word established the heavens; his word brought creation into being; his word made the angels; and you have doubts about a birth? That is why the angel was indignant and did not pardon him even on account of his priesthood. Indeed, because of it he was punished all the more severely. For the one held in greater honour than others ought also to surpass others in faith. And what was the manner of the punishment? "See, you will be silent and unable to speak." "Your tongue," he says, "which [?]"

[Variant: [?] not here, but placed inside thus: "and of men; having therefore entered into the innermost sanctuary itself, he saw." A little after this, "how he [?] the whole multitude" [?] "offering" [?] "making." [?] "Do you see" [?] some manuscripts [?] "John; and very great and seemly; for since" [?]]

…upon the earth, and makes it tremble.” Just look at the ease of the Maker! He did not [?] the earth, and yet he shook an earth so great and so vast. “He who touches the mountains, and they smoke”; “he who shakes the earth under heaven from its foundations, and its pillars totter”; “he who threatens the sea and dries it up”; “he who says to the deep, You shall be laid waste.” “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back; the mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of the flock.” All creation is shaken, is afraid, trembles. These men alone scorn, disdain and cheapen their own salvation. I would not say they cheapen the Lord of all. Before, we tried to bring them to their senses by pointing to the powers above: angels, archangels, the Cherubim, the Seraphim. Now we point to senseless creation, and even this does not shame them. Do you not see this heaven here, how beautiful it is, how great, how it is crowned with the varied chorus of the stars? How long has it lasted? It has stood for five thousand years and more, and all that time has not brought old age on it. A young and vigorous body keeps the bloom of its youth fresh and at its prime, and in the same way the heaven has kept the beauty it was given from the beginning and has grown no weaker with time. Yet this heaven, so beautiful, so great, so bright, so studded with stars, so enduring, standing for so long, was made by this God, whom you pry into and confine within the limits of your own reasonings, as easily as someone might build a hut in play. Isaiah showed this when he said, “He who set up the heaven like a vault, and stretched it out like a tent over the earth.” Do you want to look at the earth as well? He made this too as if it were nothing. Of the heaven the prophet says, “He who set up the heaven like a vault, and stretched it out like a tent over the earth.” Of the earth he says, “He who holds the circle of the earth, who made the earth as nothing.” Do you see how he called an earth so great and so vast nothing? 4. Just think how great a mass you see, how many nations of people, how many tall trees and plants in what numbers, how many cities, how many great buildings, and what multitudes of four-footed animals, wild beasts and reptiles of every kind it carries on its back. [1457] Yet he made an earth of such kind and size so easily that the prophet could not even find an illustration of that ease and said that he made the earth as nothing. The magnitude and beauty of visible things were not enough to show the Creator's power and fell far short of the greatness and strength of the one who made them all. So the prophets found another way to show us, as far as they could, something more about God's power. What way was that? They set out not only the magnitude of created things but also the manner of their creation. So from both, the magnitude of what was made and the ease of its making, we may form some worthy idea of God's power, as far as we are able. Do not, then, examine only the magnitude of what was made, but also… Do you see how he called it nothing. [?] Others read: “the cheapness” [?] “the nothingness.”

[?]… For if not prying into his promises glorifies him, then meddling with and searching out not only his decrees but even the one who decreed them dishonors him. And to see that not prying into his promises glorifies him, listen to Paul speaking about Abraham, his obedience and his faith in all things: “He considered his own body, already as good as dead, and the deadness of Sarah's womb; yet he did not waver in unbelief at the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith.” His nature and his age, Paul is saying, drove him to despair, but faith held out good hopes. “But he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, and being fully convinced that what he had promised he was able also to do.” Do you see that someone fully convinced of whatever God declares gives glory to God? If, then, the one who believes him gives glory to God, the one who disbelieves him turns the dishonor back on his own head. “Who are you to answer back to God?” Then Paul wanted to show how wide the gap between man and God is. He did not show it as fully as it deserved, but from the example he gave we can form an idea of a far greater difference. What does he say? “Will what is molded say to its molder, Why have you made me like this? Does the potter not have power over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” What are you saying? Must I be as subject to God as clay is to the potter? Yes, he says, for the gap between man and God is as great as that between clay and potter. In fact the gap is not merely that great but far greater. Clay and potter are of one substance, as Job says: “Let alone those who dwell in houses of clay, of which we ourselves are made, of the same clay.” And if a man looks better and more comely than clay, it is not a change of nature that made the difference but the skill of the craftsman. [1459] Otherwise you differ in no way from clay. If you do not believe it, let the coffins and caskets persuade you. Go to the tombs of your ancestors and you will know that this is so. Between clay and potter, then, there is no difference, but between the substance of God and that of men the gap is so great that no word can express it and no thought can measure it. Clay follows the potter's hands wherever he draws and turns it. In the same way you too must stay silent like the clay whenever God wishes to arrange something. Paul did not say this to take away our power of choice (God forbid!) or to damage our free will. He said it to curb our arrogance with a great margin to spare. If you like, let us look at this too. What was it those people wanted to learn, that he silenced them so sharply? Were they prying into God's substance? Not at all. No one ever dared to do that. They were asking something much smaller: they were inquiring into God's dispensations. Why, for instance, is one person punished while another receives mercy? Why is one person freed from punishment while another is in distress? Why did one obtain pardon and another not? These were the sorts of things they asked. How do we know this? From what comes just before. For he had said, “So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. You will say to me then, Why does he still find fault? For who [?] his will…” Others, with Savile, read “and to be searched out.” …the manner of the resurrection was shown.

…the pattern was shown. Many dead people had risen, often, even before him, but not one in this way. All the others who rose returned to the earth again. They were freed from the tyranny of death for a time, then were brought back under its rule. But the Lord's body rose and did not return to the earth. It ascended into the heavens, destroyed the whole tyranny of the enemy, raised the whole world with itself, and now sits on the royal throne. Paul had all this in mind. He wanted to show that no reasoning can explain wonders so many and so great, and that faith alone can teach them and make them clear. So he said, “by faith, that I may know the power of his resurrection.” Reasoning cannot explain even an ordinary resurrection, since that is beyond human nature and the normal course of things. What reasoning, then, could explain a resurrection that differs so much from all the others? None at all. We need faith alone if we are to be persuaded that a mortal body both rose and entered an immortal life with no limit and no end. Paul pointed to this elsewhere when he said, “Christ, being raised, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him.” So the wonder is double: that he rose, and that he rose in this way. That is why he said, “by faith, that I may know the power of his resurrection.” If the resurrection cannot be discovered by reasoning, how much less the birth from above? When Paul discussed these things and spoke of the cross and the passion, he entrusted those too to the power of faith. Then, having set this whole argument in motion, [461] he went on to say, “Brothers, I do not consider that I have laid hold of it.” He did not say, “I do not consider that I know,” but “that I have laid hold of it.” He claimed for himself neither complete ignorance nor complete knowledge. To say “I do not consider that I have laid hold of it” shows that he is still on the road, walking and pressing on, but has certainly not reached the end. He urges this on others too: “Let those of us who are mature think this way; and if you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this to you as well.” Not “reasoning will teach you,” he said, but “God will reveal it.” Do you see that the subject is not life and conduct but doctrines and faith? Conduct and life do not need revelation, but doctrines and knowledge do. Elsewhere he shows the same thing when he says, “If anyone thinks he knows anything, he has not yet known anything.” He did not simply say that such a person knows nothing, but that he does not know as he ought to know. He has knowledge, but it is not precise or complete. 7. To show you that this is true, let us not discuss the things above. If you like, let us bring the argument down to the visible creation. Do you not see this heaven here? We know that it has the shape of a vault, and we learned this not from reasonings but from divine Scripture. We also know that it encloses the whole earth, and we heard this from Scripture too. But what its substance is, we do not know. If anyone insists and argues, let him say what the heaven is in substance. Is it frozen ice? Is it condensed cloud? Others read ᾗ μέλλοιμεν, others εἰ μέλλοιμεν. Others read εἴ τι ἕτερον. [?] Others read τίς δὲ οὐσίᾳ. Below, three manuscripts read: “would have nothing clear.”

[?] On the Incomprehensible Nature of God, and that not even God's condescension can be borne by the Seraphim. Third Homily.
1. When hard-working farmers see a barren, wild tree damaging their work, its rough roots and heavy shade ruining their cultivated plants, they cut it down with great zeal. Often a wind comes from somewhere and helps with the cutting. It strikes the tree at the notch, shakes it with great force, snaps it and throws it to the ground, and spares them most of the work. We too are cutting down a wild and savage tree, the heresy of the Anomoeans. So let us ask God to send us the grace of the Spirit, so that it may strike harder than any wind, tear the heresy up by the roots, and spare us most of the work. When land is left fallow and gets no care from the farmer's hands, it throws up evil weeds, a mass of thorns and wild trees from its own bosom. In the same way the soul of the Anomoeans has been left desolate and has had no care from the Scriptures, and so from within itself [465] it has thrown up this wild and savage heresy. Paul did not plant this tree, Apollos did not water it, and God did not make it grow. The untimely curiosity of reasonings planted it, the conceit of folly watered it, and love of glory made it grow [?]. We need the flame of the Spirit, so that we may not only pull up this evil root but also burn it. Let us call on him, then, the God whom they blaspheme and we praise. Let us ask him to rouse our tongue to run a fuller course and to open our minds to a clearer unfolding of what is said. All our labor is for him and his glory, or rather for our own salvation. No one can harm God by dishonoring him, and no one can make him more glorious by praising him. He always remains in his own glory, neither increased by praise nor diminished by blasphemy. But among men, those who glorify him as he deserves reap the benefit of their praise. In truth no one can glorify him as he deserves; they glorify him as far as they are able. Those who blaspheme and belittle him ruin their own salvation. Someone said of blasphemers, “He who throws a stone on high throws it on his own head.” A man who hurls a stone at the sky cannot pierce the body of the sky or even reach that height; the stone comes back to the one who threw it, and he takes the blow on his own head. In the same way, someone who blasphemes that blessed substance could never harm [?] it, since it is far greater and higher than [?] the understanding of what is said.

…of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.” Does he do this only for the Father and not for the Son? Listen to how he did the very same thing for the Only-begotten. After saying, “I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh,” he added, “to them belong the adoption, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship and the promises; from them, according to the flesh, comes Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen.” As he did for the Father, so for the Only-begotten he first gave the doxology and only then went on with the rest of his argument. For he had heard Christ say, “so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” And to show you that this prayer itself will give us the proof, let us bring it out into the open: “The King of kings,” he says, “and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light.” Stop here and ask the heretic what this means, “dwelling in unapproachable light,” and notice Paul's precision. He did not say “being unapproachable light” but “dwelling in unapproachable light.” He wanted you to learn that if the dwelling is unapproachable, then the God who dwells in it is much more so. He said this not so that you would imagine a house or a place around God, but so that you would learn, with a great margin to spare, that God is incomprehensible. Nor did he say “dwelling in incomprehensible light,” but “unapproachable,” which is far greater than incomprehensible. We call something incomprehensible when people search and look for it and do not grasp it. Unapproachable is what does not allow itself to be searched at all, [465] and no one can even come near it. For example, we call a sea incomprehensible when divers let themselves down into it, sink to a great depth, and cannot find the bottom. But we call unapproachable what cannot even be sought or searched at all. 3. What would you say to this? “But it is incomprehensible to men,” he says, “not to angels or to the powers above.” Tell me, are you an angel? Do you belong to the choir of bodiless powers? Are you not a man, of the same substance as I am? Or have you forgotten your own nature? Let us suppose that it is unapproachable to men only, although this is not added. Paul did not say, “dwelling in light unapproachable to men but not to angels.” Still, if you like, let us grant it for argument's sake. Are you not yourself a man? So even if it is not unapproachable to angels, what is that to you? You are the one who argues, pries, and claims that that substance can be comprehended by human nature. But to show you that it is unapproachable not only to men but also to the powers above, listen to what Isaiah says. When I say Isaiah, I mean the declaration of the Spirit, for every prophet speaks what the Spirit works in him: “And it came to pass in the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, and the Seraphim stood around him. Each had six wings, and each had six wings, and with two they covered their faces and with two their feet.” For what reason [?]… [?] and some manuscripts read μηδὲ ἐρευνᾶσθαι ἀνέχεται. Others, with Savile, read μηδὲ ἐρεύνης ἀνέχεται. Others read τοῦ ἐνιαυτοῦ. [?] …then Daniel.

…his arms and his legs like the appearance of gleaming bronze, and the sound of his words like the sound of a multitude. And I alone saw this vision, and those who were with me did not see it, but a great terror fell on them and they fled in fear. No strength was left in me, and my glory was turned to corruption.” What does “my glory was turned to corruption” mean? Daniel was a handsome young man. The fear of the angel's presence put him in the state of a dying man: it made him very pale, used up the bloom of his youth, and drained all the healthy color from his face. That is why he says, “My glory was turned to corruption.” When a charioteer takes fright and lets go of the reins, all the horses plunge headlong and the whole chariot overturns. The same thing usually happens to the soul when it is gripped by amazement and anguish. In its terror it draws back its own energies from each of the body's senses, as if pulling in the reins, and leaves the limbs abandoned. Then the limbs, deprived of the power that held them together, collapse and are knocked about. This is what Daniel suffered then. What did the angel do? He raised him up and said, “Daniel, man greatly beloved, understand the words that I speak to you, and stand upright, for I have now been sent to you.” And he stood up trembling. When the angel began to speak with him again and said, “From the first day that you set your heart to humble yourself before God, your words were heard, and I have come because of your words,” he fell to the ground again. This also happens to people who faint. They come round and return to themselves and look about, while we hold them and sprinkle their faces with cold water, and then they often faint again in our very hands. The prophet suffered the same thing. His soul was terrified. It could not bear the sight of the presence of a fellow servant, nor could it endure that light, and so it was in turmoil, straining to break free from the bond of the flesh as if from a chain. But the angel still held him. Let those who pry into the Lord of the angels hear this. Daniel, whom even the eyes of lions respected, Daniel, who achieved superhuman things in a human body, could not bear the presence of a fellow servant, but lay there without breath. “For my insides were turned over at my vision,” he says, “and no breath was left in me.” Yet these men, who fall so far short of that righteous man's virtue, promise to know with complete precision the very substance that is highest and first, the substance that brought into being these myriads of angels. Daniel could not bear to see even one of them. 5. But let us bring the argument back to our earlier subject and show that God cannot be seen even by the powers above, even when he condescends. Tell me, why do the Seraphim hold their wings in front of them? For no other reason than to proclaim in advance, by what they do, the apostle's words “dwelling in unapproachable light.” And not they alone, but also those ranked above them, the Cherubim. The Seraphim stand nearby, but the Cherubim are the throne of God. This is not because God needs a throne, but so that through this [?]… Others read προβάλλονται. [?] …not so that you would imagine a throne, for he does not need a throne. [?] Others read: “is able to see with confidence, where.”

6. I also wanted to show now that God is incomprehensible not only to the Cherubim and the Seraphim, but also to the principalities, the powers, and every other created power. But my mind has grown weary, not because so much has been said but because what has been said is so awesome. For the soul trembles and is struck with amazement when it lingers long over the contemplation of things above. So come, let us bring it down from the heavens and refresh it in its amazement by turning to our usual exhortation. And what is that? That we pray for those who suffer from such diseases to be healed some day. For if we are commanded to entreat God for those who are sick, for those in the mines and in harsh slavery, and for the possessed, how much more for these? Impiety is worse even than a demon. That madness has some excuse, but this disease has no defence at all. But since I have mentioned the prayer for the possessed, I want to discuss something with your love and to cut out a grievous disease of the Church. For it would be absurd for us to treat outsiders with such care and to neglect our own members. What, then, is the disease? This countless multitude, now gathered together and attending so carefully to what is said, I have often looked for at that most awesome hour and could not find it, and I have groaned deeply. When a fellow servant is speaking there is great zeal and intense eagerness, as people push against one another and stay to the end. But when Christ is about to appear in the holy mysteries, the church becomes empty and deserted. How can this deserve pardon? Through this laziness you lose all the praise you earned for your zeal in listening. For who will not condemn both you and us, when he sees the fruit of your listening at once drain away? If you had attended carefully to what was said, you would have shown your zeal by your deeds. But to bolt as soon as you have heard is a sign that you have received nothing of what was said and stored none of it in your minds. If the words had been stored up in your souls, they would surely have kept you inside and led you with greater piety to the most awesome rites. As it is, you leave as though you had been listening to a lyre-player, without any benefit at all, once the speaker stops. But what is the feeble excuse of the many? 'I can pray at home,' one says, 'but I cannot hear a homily and teaching at home.' You deceive yourself, man. It is possible to pray at home, but it is impossible to pray at home as one prays in church, where there is so great a multitude of fathers, where a cry is sent up to God with one accord. You are not heard as well when you entreat the Master by yourself as when you do so with your brothers. For here there is something more: concord and harmony, the bond of love, and the prayers of the priests. This is why the priests preside, so that the prayers of the multitude, which are weaker, may lay hold of these stronger ones and rise together with them into heaven. Besides, what good would a homily be if prayer were not joined to it? First comes prayer, and then the word. So too the apostles say: 'But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.' Paul does the same, praying at the beginning of his letters, so that, like the light of a lamp, the light of prayer [?] Other manuscripts read 'reverence'. [?] of the devil's tyranny.

[?] we pray for these, whom you yourself first deigned to love so greatly that you gave up your own life for them. For these we pour out our supplications, for whom you yourself shed your blood. For these we entreat, for whom you sacrificed this body. That is why, at that time, the deacon has the possessed stand and bids them only bow their heads and make their supplications through the posture of their bodies, for it is not lawful for them to pray with the common assembly of the brethren. That is why he has them stand: so that you may take pity on them, both for their misfortune and for their speechlessness, and use your own boldness of speech to plead their cause. Considering all these things, then, let us run together at that hour, so that we may draw down mercy and find grace for timely [?] Other manuscripts read 'to them'. [?] unto the ages of ages. Amen.

By the same author, On the Incomprehensible, against the Anomoeans. Fourth Homily.

1. Having shown the other day that God is incomprehensible to human beings, and also to the Cherubim and the Seraphim, it would have been enough to be done with the matter and stir nothing further. But our whole eagerness and zeal is not only to sew shut the mouths of our opponents but also to make your love wiser, so we take up the same subject again and carry the discussion further. Spending time on these matters will make you know more, and it will make our victory more brilliant by clearing away whatever remnant may still be left. For bad weeds must not merely be cut off at the top, since they sprout again while their roots lie below. They must be pulled out from the very flanks and bosom of the earth and laid bare to the heat of the sun's rays, so that they wither easily. Come, then, let us lead you up to heaven again by our discourse. We do not do this out of meddling or idle curiosity. We are hastening to put an end to the untimely contentiousness of those who do not know themselves and will not bear to know the limits of human nature. That is why, out of great abundance, we showed that not only the appearance of God but even that of angels was unbearable to that righteous man, when we read you the whole story and kept showing you the blessed Daniel growing pale and trembling, in no better state than men at their last breath, his soul hastening to break the bond of the flesh. For just as a tame and gentle dove kept in a little house, when it senses something fearful, flies up in terror to the ceiling and looks for a way out through the windows, eager to escape its distress, so the soul of that blessed man hastened to fly out of the body, pressed outward on every side, and went out [?] we lead you up to heaven again. And this we do

[?] Paul said this, not to confine God to a place, but so that his incomprehensibility and inaccessibility might shine forth all the more abundantly. We also brought forward other powers, the Cherubim, and showed how above them there was a firmament, a crystal stone, the likeness of a throne, the form of a man, amber, fire, and a bow. After all those things the prophet says: 'This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.' Through all these things we showed you God's condescension, and that even this is unbearable to the powers above.

2. I am not recapitulating these things for no reason. Since I owe you the debt of that promise, I want to learn exactly what I have paid and what remains. That is what people who owe loans do: they bring the bond out into the open, where the whole account is written, show it to their creditors, and pay what remains. So I too will unroll the memory of your minds like a book, point with my word, as with a finger, to what has been paid, and go on to what remains. What, then, was left? To show that neither principalities, nor powers, nor dominions, nor any other created power has exact comprehension of God. For there are, there truly are, other powers whose very names we do not know. Consider the madness of the heretics: we do not even know the names of the servants, and they pry into the very essence of the Master! There are angels and archangels, thrones and dominions, principalities and powers. But these are not the only peoples in heaven. There are countless nations and unspeakable tribes, which no word can describe. And how is it clear that there are more powers than these, whose names we do not know? Paul, who spoke of these, also says this when he speaks of Christ: 'He seated him far above every principality and power and might and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come.' Do you see that there are some names there which will become known, though they are unknown now? That is why he said, 'not only named in this age but also in the age to come.' And what wonder is it if they lack exact comprehension of the essence? That is no great thing to demonstrate. These very powers above, the principalities and powers and dominions, do not know many of his dispensations. This too we shall demonstrate from the apostle's own words: they learned some of his dispensations along with us and did not know them before us. And not only did they learn them with us; they also learned them through us. 'For in other generations it was not made known,' he says, 'as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets, that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of his promise' (the promises had been given to the Jews) 'through the gospel, of which I, Paul, became a minister.' And whence [?] he speaks of comprehension and clear knowledge. How is it clear that the powers above learned this only now? For what has been said was said about human beings. Listen, then. 'To me,' he says, 'the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ.' What does 'unsearchable' mean? That which cannot be searched out. And not only that which cannot be found, but that which cannot even be tracked. Let them listen again [?] Many manuscripts read 'of all the saints'; Morel [?] 'of all men'.

[?] weakness. John, however, does not say 'No one has ever seen God' only about human beings. That was already clear from what had been said before: I mean the prophetic saying, 'I multiplied visions, and by the hands of the prophets I was represented in likenesses,' and also the declaration made to Moses. For when Moses desired to see him with his own eyes, God said: 'No one shall see my face and live.' So this was clear to us and agreed upon. John, then, says 'No one has ever seen God' not only about our nature but also about the powers above. That is why he brings in the Only-begotten as the teacher of this doctrine. Lest anyone say, 'How is this clear?' he added: 'The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.' In this way he brings in a trustworthy witness and teacher of the doctrine. Indeed, if he had only wanted to point us to what Moses said, there would have been no need to say that the Only-begotten made him known. For not only did the Only-begotten make this known; even before John said these things, having heard them from the Only-begotten, the prophet had made it clear to us, having heard it from God. But since John was going to reveal to us more than had been said then, namely that not even the powers above see him, he brings in the Only-begotten as teacher. Take 'seeing' here to mean knowledge. The bodiless powers have no pupils, eyes or eyelashes. What sight is for us, knowledge is for them. So when you hear 'No one has ever seen God,' take it that you are hearing that no one has known God in his essence with complete exactness. And when you hear that the Seraphim turned away their eyes and walled off their sight, and that the Cherubim did the same, do not think of eyes or pupils, for that shape belongs to bodies. Believe that through these things the prophet is hinting at their knowledge. So when the prophet says that they could not bear to see God condescending, he is saying nothing other than this: they cannot bear clear and exact knowledge and comprehension of him, nor do they dare to gaze steadily at the pure and unmixed essence, nor even at the condescension itself. And to gaze steadily means to know. That is why the evangelist, knowing that it is beyond human nature to know such things, and that God is incomprehensible even to the powers above, brings forward as our teacher of this doctrine the very one who sits at his right hand and knows these things exactly. And he did not simply say 'the Son,' though even that would have been enough to muzzle the mouths of the shameless. For just as many are called christs, but the true Christ is one, and many are called lords, but the Lord is one, and many are called gods, but God is one, so too many are called sons, but the Son is one. The addition of the article is enough to show that the Only-begotten is unique. Still, John was not content with this. Having said, 'No one has ever seen God,' he added, 'The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.' He said 'Only-begotten' first and then 'Son,' because many diminish his glory on account of sharing the name, [making him] one of the [?] [?] for not [?] made known [?] Other manuscripts read 'teacher of the matter', others 'teacher of the doctrine'. Shortly after, others read 'set down the words'.

[?] all these things have demonstrated to us. It remains, then, to show that the Son and the Holy Spirit alone know him with complete exactness. But let us put this off to another discourse, so as not to bury the memory of what has been said under too much material, and let us turn our discourse back to our usual exhortation. And what was our usual exhortation? To hold fast to earnest prayer with a sober mind and a wakeful soul. The other day, after I had spoken about this, I saw all of you readily obey. It would be absurd to reproach the lazy and not praise those who do well. So today I want to praise you and repay you for that obedience. The repayment will be this: I will teach you why that prayer comes before the others, and why at that time the deacon orders the demoniacs, those held fast by that evil madness, to be brought in and to bow their heads. Why, then, does he do this? The working of demons is an evil and grievous chain, a chain stronger than any iron. When a judge is about to come out and take his seat on a lofty tribunal, the jailers bring all the inmates out of the prison and seat them before the railings and curtains of the courtroom, squalid, filthy, long-haired and dressed in rags. In the same way the Fathers ordained that, when Christ is about to take his seat, as it were, on a lofty tribunal and appear in the mysteries themselves, the demoniacs should be brought in like prisoners. They are not brought in to give account of their offences, as those prisoners are, nor to undergo punishment and penalty. They are brought in so that, while the people and the whole city are present inside, common supplications may be made for them, with everyone asking the common Master with one accord on their behalf and entreating him to have mercy with intense

[?] such prayer, and at that time they spend their time outside. But now I want to reproach those who stay inside. I do not reproach them for staying inside, but because, though they stay, they are no better than those spending their time outside, since they chat with one another at that most awesome time. What are you doing, man? You see so many of your brothers standing near you as prisoners, and you talk about matters that are none of your concern? Is the sight alone not enough to strike you with awe and move you to compassion? Your brother is in chains, and you take your ease? Tell me, what pardon will you have, being so unfeeling, so inhuman, so cruel? Are you not afraid that, while you chat, lazy and careless, some demon may leap out of one of them, find your soul unoccupied and swept clean, and enter with complete freedom, finding the house without a door? At that hour all of us together ought to let fountains of tears flow, the eyes of all ought to be seen wet with weeping, and laments and wailing ought to rise from the whole church. After they shared in the mysteries, after they enjoyed the washing of baptism, after they enlisted with Christ, that wolf was able to snatch lambs from the flock and hold them in his power, and you see the calamity and do not weep? How can this be defended? You do not want to grieve with your brother? Then at least fear for yourself and rouse yourself. If you saw your neighbour's house on fire, tell me, even if that neighbour were your worst enemy, would you not run to put out the fire, for fear that it might spread and reach your own doors too? So it is with the demoniacs [?] Other manuscripts read 'it remains to say that'. One reads 'hasten for yourself and rouse yourself'. Two have 'in addition to the sacred delight at'.

[?] pressed together like one body and fixed with great attention on what is said, he did not dare send in any of his servants to lead you away from listening by advice and persuasion. He knew that none of you would put up with anyone who advised such a thing. Instead he mingled thieves and pickpockets in the crowd and arranged for many of those gathered here to have the gold they had tied up stolen from them. This has happened here many times and to many people. So that this may not happen, and so that the loss of money may not in time quench your eagerness to listen, since many suffer it, I urge and advise all of you not to come in here carrying gold. Then your zeal for listening will not become an opportunity for their crimes, and the pleasure you get from spending time here will not be darkened by the theft of your money. The devil contrived this not to make you poorer, but so that the loss of money would fill you with great disgust and lead you away from your eagerness to listen. He stripped Job of all his possessions too, not to make him poorer, but to strip him of his piety. His aim was not to take away money, for he knows that money is nothing. It was to throw the soul into sin by taking the money away. If he cannot do that, he will think he has accomplished nothing at all. So, beloved, since you know his intention, when he takes away your gold, whether through thieves or by some other means, glorify the Master, and [?] Most manuscripts read thus; Morel reads 'the theft of money [?] darkened'. Savile and two manuscripts read: 'and even if some other misfortune should assail you. For the nature of these things not only will not harm you'.

On the Incomprehensible, against the Anomoeans. Fifth Homily.

1. When someone is about to take up a lengthy subject, one that needs many words and is completed not in one day, or two, or three, but in many more, I think he must not lay the whole teaching on his hearers' minds all at once. He should cut the whole into many parts and so make the burden of the discourse light and easy to grasp by dividing it up. For the tongue, the hearing and each of our senses have fixed measures, rules and limits, and if anyone ever tries to overstep these limits, he loses even the power he has. Tell me, what is sweeter than light? What is more pleasant than a sunbeam? Yet this sweet and pleasant thing, when it meets our eyes beyond our measure, becomes oppressive and burdensome. That is why God ordained that night should follow day. Night takes over our tired eyes, closes the eyelids, puts the pupils to sleep and rests our weary power of sight, making it better fit to view the coming day. That is why waking and sleep, though opposites, are both most pleasant when kept in due proportion. Just as we call light sweet, so we also call sweet the

…angels, nor archangels, nor the powers above: he made this plain by what he added. For after saying, "Not that anyone has ever seen the Father," he went on, "except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father." Had he simply said "no one," many of his hearers might perhaps have thought it was said only of our human nature. But by saying "no one" and adding "except the Son," he shut out the whole of creation through that addition about the Only-begotten. "What then," someone says, "about the Holy Spirit?" Not at all. The Spirit is no part of creation either, and "no one" is always used to set creation alone apart. When it is said of the Father it does not push out the Son, and when it is said of the Son it does not cast out the Spirit. To make this very point clear here and now, that "no one" is said not to set aside the Spirit but to set creation apart, let us hear what Paul says to the Corinthians about this same knowledge, which Christ says belongs to the Son alone. What, then, does he say? "For who knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him? So too no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God." Just as here the word "no one" does not cast out the Son, so too in Christ's saying the word "no one" does not push out the Holy Spirit. This shows that what I said is true. For if, when Christ said, "No one has seen the Father except the one who is from God," the Spirit were pushed out, Paul would have said to no purpose that, as a man knows his own affairs, so the Holy Spirit knows the things of God with exactness. The word "one" is used in the same way, for it has the same force and meaning as "no one." Consider: "There is one God," he says, "the Father, from whom are all things, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things." If calling the Father "one God" casts the Son out of the Godhead, then calling the Son "one Lord" casts the Father out of the lordship. But calling Jesus Christ "one Lord" certainly does not cast the Father out of the lordship. So neither does calling the Father "one God" cast the Son out of the Godhead.

2. But suppose they say again that the Father is called "one God" because, although the Son is God, he is not God in the way the Father is. Then it follows from their own premises (we would never say it ourselves) that the Son is called "one Lord" because, although the Father is Lord, he is not Lord in the way the Son is. If that is impious, the former claim cannot stand either. Just as "one Lord" does not push the Father out of true lordship, nor confine it to the Son alone, so "one God" does not cast the Son out of true, genuine and pure Godhead, nor show that it belongs to the Father alone. For that the Son is God, and God of the same kind as the Father, while remaining Son, from [?] … [?] Paul says to the Corinthians: "What then does he say? For who knows…" [?] Some read "inferior."

…our [God]; no other shall be reckoned beside him," he went on: "He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among men." And Paul says, "From them, according to the flesh, is the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen." And again: "No fornicator or covetous person has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God." And again: "At the appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ." John too calls him this, saying, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

3. "Yes," someone says, "but show me where Scripture ranks him with the Father and calls the Father Lord." I will show not only this, but that it calls the Father Lord and the Son Lord, and calls the Father God and the Son God, setting both names side by side. Where can this be found? Once, in discussion with the Jews, Christ says, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They say to him, "David's." He says to them, "How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying, The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand?" There you have Lord and Lord. Do you want to learn where Scripture calls the Father and the Son God and God, setting them side by side? Hear the prophet David and the apostle Paul showing us this very thing: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of your kingdom is a scepter of uprightness. You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." And Paul in turn cited this testimony, saying, "Of the angels he says, Who makes his angels spirits; but of the Son, Your throne, O God, is forever and ever."

"Why then," someone says, "did he call the Father God in that passage, and the Son Lord?" He did not do it there idly or at random, but because he was addressing Greeks sick with polytheism. So that they could not say that he, while charging them with speaking of many gods and many lords, was himself caught in the same charge by speaking of gods and not of God, he stooped to their weakness and called the Son by another name with the same force. To show that this is true, let us read the passage itself from the beginning, and you will see clearly that what I say is no guess of mine: "Now concerning food offered to idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. As to the eating of food offered to idols, then, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is no other God but one." Do you see that he says this with his eye on those who thought there were many gods? "For although there are so-called gods, [and many lords,] whether in heaven or on earth" (again he is fighting them), "as indeed there are many gods and many lords" (that is, so-called ones), "yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are [all things]…" [?] setting side by side [?]. Others read: [?] again he adduced this testimony concerning Christ, saying that. Others read: "knows."

…of ours is in the body, not even this can we say. For what could anyone say? That it is stretched out through the bulk of the body? But that is absurd, for this is a property of bodies. That it is not so with the soul is clear from this: often, when the hands and feet have been cut off, the soul remains whole, in no way maimed by the mutilation of the body. Is it, then, not in the whole body but confined to some part? Then the other limbs must be dead, for what has no soul is certainly dead. But we cannot say this either. We know that the soul is in our body, but how it is there we do not know. This is why God has shut us out even from knowledge of the soul, in his great bounty curbing and restraining us, persuading us to stay below and not to pry curiously or meddle with things above us.

But so that we may not build such arguments on reasoning alone, let us bring the discussion back to Scripture. "Not that anyone has seen the Father," he says, "except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father." "And what does that prove?" someone says. "This saying does not yet testify that he has exact knowledge." He showed that creation does not know him when he said, "Not that anyone has seen the Father"; and he showed that the Son knows him when he added, "except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father." But that he knows him exactly, and as the Father knows himself, has not yet been proved. "For it is possible," he says, "that neither creation knows him clearly nor the Son, but that the Son knows him more clearly than creation does, yet does not have exact comprehension either. He said that the Son sees and knows what the Father is, but that he knows him exactly, and as the Father knows himself, he has not yet shown." Do you want us, then, to confirm this too from the Scriptures, and from Christ's own voice? Then let us hear what he says to the Jews: "As the Father knows me, so I know the Father." What knowledge more exact than this do you still want? Ask your opponent: "Does the Father know the Son exactly? Does he have full and exact knowledge of him? Is nothing about the Son hidden from him, and is his knowing complete?" "Yes," he says. Then when you hear that the Son knows the Father as the Father knows the Son, seek nothing further, since their knowledge is equal in exactness. Elsewhere too he showed the same thing when he said, "No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him." But he reveals him not as far as he himself knows him, but as far as we can take in. If Paul does this, much more does Christ. For Paul says to his own disciples, "I could not speak to you as spiritual people but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not yet able." "But he said this only to the Corinthians," someone says. What then if we show that he also knew certain other things which no human being had learned, and departed as the only one of all men who knew them? And where can this be found? In the Epistle to the Corinthians; for he is the one who says, [?] become parts [?]. Five manuscripts read: "knowing also other things … had already learned." [?] where concerning the nature of bodies.

…to go over the whole of it measuring with the span of the hand, whom shall we say knows the size of heaven: the one who insists that he knows how many spans it has, or the one who admits he does not know? Then, if in the case of heaven the one who yields before its size is the one who knows its size better, shall we not use even this reverence in the case of God? How is this not the height of madness? To show that all that is required of us is to know that God exists, not to pry into his essence, hear what Paul says: "Whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists." And again, when the prophet charges someone with impiety, his charge is not that he does not know what God is, but that he does not know that God exists. "The fool," he says, "has said in his heart, There is no God." Just as what makes that man impious is not ignorance of what God is in essence, but ignorance that God exists, so for piety it is enough to know that God exists.

But they have another argument they have rehearsed. What is it? "It has been said," they say, "that God is spirit." Tell me, does this set forth his essence? Who could put up with such talk, if he had come anywhere near the doors of the divine Scriptures? For by this reasoning God will also be fire. For just as it is written that God is spirit, so it is written, "Our God is a consuming fire," and again, "[?] of living water." And he will be not only spirit and fountain and fire, but also soul, and wind, and the human mind, and other things far more absurd than these. There is no need to go through them all in my discourse, nor to imitate those people's madness. For the word "spirit" means many things. It means our soul, as Paul says: "Hand such a man over to Satan, so that the spirit may be saved." It means wind, as the prophet says: "With a violent wind may he shatter them." The spiritual gift is also called this: "The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit," he says; and again, "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also." Anger too is called this, for Isaiah says, "Were you not the one who planned with your harsh spirit to destroy them?" The help that comes from God is also called spirit: "The breath of our face, Christ the Lord." So by their account our God will be all these things, and will be made up of so many.

But so that we may not talk nonsense by bringing forward things that do not even need refuting, let us end our argument against them here and turn wholly to prayer, beseeching and begging all the more for them the more impious they are, that they may at last turn from their madness. For this is acceptable in the sight of God our Savior, who wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

6. Let us not cease, then, to make supplication for them. For prayer is a great weapon, an unfailing treasure, wealth that is never spent, a harbor without waves, a ground of calm. Prayer is the root, the fountain and the mother of countless blessings, and it is mightier even than kingship. Often, when the very man who wears the diadem is in a fever, lying on his bed and burning, doctors, bodyguards, servants and generals stand around him, and neither the doctors' skill, nor the presence of friends, nor the service of household slaves, nor an abundance of drugs, nor [?] … Others read "touch." Soon after, others read "calm." [?] works the place.

…[?]. And yet it is not even humility for one who is a sinner to think that he is a sinner. Humility is when someone who is conscious of many great deeds imagines nothing great about himself; when someone like Paul, who can say, "I am not aware of anything against myself," says in turn, "but I am not thereby justified," and again, "Christ Jesus came to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost." This is humility: to be lofty in achievements and to humble oneself in mind. Yet God, in his unspeakable love for mankind, welcomes and receives not only the humble but also those who frankly confess their sins, and he becomes gracious and kind to those so disposed.

To learn how good it is to imagine nothing great about oneself, build two chariots in your mind. Yoke righteousness with arrogance, and sin with humility, and you will see the team of sin outrun righteousness, not by its own strength but by the strength of its yokefellow humility; and the other team falling behind, not through the weakness of righteousness but through the weight and bulk of arrogance. For just as humility, by its surpassing height, overcomes the heaviness of sin and gets up to heaven first, so arrogance, by its great weight and bulk, can overpower even the lightest righteousness and easily drag it down.

7. To see that this team is faster than the other, remember the Pharisee and the tax collector. The Pharisee yoked righteousness with arrogance, speaking like this: "I thank you, O God, that I am not like the rest of men, robbers, grasping, or even like this tax collector." What madness! The whole human race was not enough to sate his arrogance; with great folly he leapt even upon the tax collector standing nearby. What then did the tax collector do? He did not beat off the insults or smart at the accusation, but accepted what was said with good grace. And the enemy's arrow became a medicine and a cure for him, the insult became praise, and the accusation a crown. So fine a thing is humility, so great a gain, not to be stung by others' abuse nor turned savage by our neighbors' insults. For from these too one can reap a great and noble good, as happened with the tax collector. He accepted the insults and laid aside his sins, and by saying, "Be merciful to me, a sinner," he went down justified rather than the other. Words prevailed over works, and speech defeated deeds. For the one [?] righteous [?] … [?] human [?] … [?] arrogance [?] surpassing [?] … [?] that I am not like the rest of men, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week; I give tithes of all that I get. [?] What are you saying, wretch? [?] boasting about fasting [?] sick with such contempt [?] your surpassing [?] … you strain out the gnat but swallow the camel [?] … calling yourself [?], do you not know what is written? [?] … But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, but beat his breast, saying, "God, be merciful to me, a sinner." [?] of humble words, and at once the crown [?] … [?] Pharisee. "I tell you, this man went down to his house justified [?]" … [?] loves, and assents to your supplications. This then

is the very thing Christ was showing when he said, "Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest." He calls, then; let us not turn a deaf ear. He draws us; let us not leap away. Even if we have countless sins, let us run to him all the more then, for it is such people he calls. "For I came," he says, "to call not the righteous but sinners to repentance." Here too he means the burdened, the wearied, those exhausted by the weight of their sins. For he is called the God of consolation and the God of compassion, since it is his unceasing work to comfort and console those who are in pain and distress, even if they have countless sins. Only let us give ourselves up to him, only let us run to him and not draw away, and by experience itself we shall know the truth of what has been said, and nothing in the world will be able to grieve us, if we have [?]

On the blessed Philogonius, who became a bishop after being an advocate; and that nothing equals care for the common good in winning favor with God; and that approaching the divine mysteries carelessly brings unbearable punishment, even if we dare to do it only once a year. Delivered five days before the Nativity of Christ. Sixth Discourse.

1. Today too I was preparing to strip for the wrestling bouts with the heretics and to pay you the rest of what I owe. But the day of the blessed Philogonius, whose feast we are now keeping, has called our tongue to tell of his achievements, and we must certainly obey. For if he who speaks ill of father or mother [?] … having gone up to heaven, he would need nothing of human

praise, since he has departed to a greater and more blessed lot. But we who are still turning about here, and need much encouragement from every side, need his praises, so that we may be roused to the same zeal. This is why a wise man counsels us, saying, "The memory of the righteous is with praises"; not because the departed benefit from it, but because those who praise them gain the greatest benefit. Since, then, we gain so much from the practice, let us obey and not object; for the occasion too is fitting for such an account. Today the blessed man passed over to the life free from turmoil and anchored his ship where there is no longer any shipwreck to fear, nor any despondency or pain. And what wonder is it if that place is free of despondency, when Paul, speaking to people still alive, says, "Rejoice always; pray without ceasing"? If here, where there are diseases and abuse and untimely deaths, slanders and envy, despondency and anger, evil desires and countless plots, daily cares, and evils coming one after another without a break and bringing countless griefs on every side, Paul said it was possible to rejoice always, if one lifts one's head a little out of the storm of worldly affairs and orders one's own life well, then much more after our departure from here is it easy to attain this good, when all these things have been done away with—sicknesses, passions and every occasion of sin—when "mine" and "yours" no longer exist, that chilling phrase which brings every evil into our life and has bred countless wars.

This above all is why I count this saint blessed: though he has moved on and left the city we live in, he has gone up to another city, the city of God; though he has left this Church, he is enrolled in that Church of the firstborn who are registered in heaven; and though he has left these feasts behind, he has passed over to the festal gathering of the angels. For to show that there is a city above, and a Church, and a festal gathering, hear Paul saying, "You have come to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the Church of the firstborn who are registered in heaven, and to myriads of angels in festal gathering." He calls everything there a festal gathering not only because of the multitude of the powers above, but also because of the abundance of good things and the unceasing joy and gladness. For what usually makes a festal fair is nothing other than the crowd of people gathered and the plenty of goods for sale, when wheat and barley and every kind of produce, flocks of sheep and herds of cattle, clothing and other such things are brought in, some people selling and others buying. "And which of these things is in heaven?" someone says. None of these, but things far more august. Not wheat and barley and kinds of produce, but everywhere there the fruit of the Spirit: love and joy and gladness and peace and goodness and gentleness in great abundance. Not flocks of sheep and herds of cattle, but spirits [?] … Others read: "the multitude of those coming together, and the…" [?] [made] perfect, and the virtues of saints and the achievements of the elect. [?]

…to do the same as the rich. For when they receive small gifts from the poor, things they have no need of, they add gifts of their own and so repay those who brought what they had. In the same way he too, receiving from us praise in words, which he does not need, will give us in return blessing through deeds, which we always need. Where, then, should we begin our praises? Where else than from the office that the grace of the Spirit entrusted to him? Worldly offices are by no means proof of the virtue of those entrusted with them; often they even accuse them of wickedness. Why? Because the patronage of friends, canvassing, flattery and many other things more shameful than these usually procure such offices. But when God ordains and casts the vote, and that hand touches the holy head, the vote cannot be bribed, the judgment is above suspicion, and the dignity of the one ordaining is indisputable proof of the worth of the one ordained. That it was God who ordained him is clear from the very manner of it. He was snatched from the middle of the marketplace and led to this throne. So dignified and splendid was the life he had led before, and though he had a wife and a daughter and was busy in the law courts, he shone so far above the sun that straight from there he was found worthy of this office, and was led from the judge's tribunal to the sacred tribunal. Then he pleaded for men against men who plotted against them, making the wronged stronger than those who wronged them; but when he came here he pleaded for men against the demons who abuse them. How great a sign of virtue it is to be deemed worthy of so great an office by the grace of God, hear from what the risen Christ says to Peter. When he asked him, "Peter, do you love me?" and Peter answered, "Lord, you know that I love you," Christ did not say: throw away your money, practice fasting and hardship, raise the dead, drive out demons. He brought up none of these, neither the other signs nor the other achievements; passing over all of them, he says, "If you love me, tend my sheep." He said this not only because he wished to show us the greatest sign of love for him, but also because of the love he shows for the sheep; he has made this the greatest proof of goodwill toward himself, all but saying: whoever loves my sheep loves me.
