See how much Christ endured for this flock: he became man, took the form of a servant, was spat upon and struck; and at last he did not even refuse death, and a shameful death at that, for he poured out his blood on a cross. So if anyone wishes to win his approval, let him take care of these sheep, seek the common good, and look after his brothers; for no achievement is more precious to God than this. That is why he says elsewhere: "Simon, Simon, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail." What return, then, do you give me for this care and providence? What return do you ask for? This same thing again: "And you," he says, "when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers." So too Paul says: "Be imitators of me," [?] … shameful, but even the blood itself.

…he sent down the Spirit, which is Pentecost. So from here, as from a spring, various rivers have flowed, and these feasts have been born for us. Not only for this reason would this day justly enjoy precedence, but also because what happened on it is far more awe-inspiring than all the rest. That Christ, having become man, should die followed as a consequence; for though he committed no sin, he did take a mortal body. That too was marvelous. But that he, being God, should will to become man and should consent to descend so far that the mind cannot even grasp it, this is the most awe-inspiring thing of all and full of amazement. Paul marveled at this when he said, "And by common confession great is the mystery of godliness." What is great? "God was manifested in the flesh." And again elsewhere: "For God does not take hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham; therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect." That is why I embrace and love this day above all, and set my love before you, so that I may make you sharers in my affection. That is why I beg and entreat all of you with all earnestness and eagerness to come, each of you emptying his own house, so that we may see our Master lying in the manger, wrapped in swaddling clothes, that awesome and wondrous sight. What defense will we have, what pardon, if he comes down from heaven for our sake and we do not even come from our homes to him? If magi, barbarians and foreigners, run from Persia to see him lying in the manger, while you, a Christian, will not put up with even a short journey to enjoy this blessed sight? For if we come with faith, we will certainly see him lying in the manger, since this table takes the place of the manger.

For here too the Master's body will lie, not wrapped in swaddling clothes as it was then, but clothed on every side by the Holy Spirit. The initiated know what I mean. The magi only worshiped; but you, if you come with a pure conscience, we will even allow to take it and go home. So you too come and bring gifts, not such as theirs, but far more sacred. They offered gold; you offer self-control and virtue. They offered frankincense; you offer pure prayers, the spiritual incense. They offered myrrh; you offer humility, a humbled heart, and almsgiving. If you come with these gifts, you will enjoy this sacred table with great confidence. I am raising these points now because I know that many will certainly come on that day and fall upon this spiritual sacrifice. So that we may do this not to our harm or to the condemnation of our souls, but for our salvation, I solemnly warn you now in advance and urge you to purify yourselves in every way and only then approach the sacred mysteries.

4. And let no one say to me, "I am full of shame, I am sinful…"

[Some manuscripts read prosedrias, others proedrias.]

…the distance is great [?], if we are willing. There is no need to cross a sea, or to climb over mountain peaks [?] … brings punishment for negligence. Do you not know that this … of fire [?] … but sitting at home, showing reverence and [?] … the table is full of spiritual [?], and like springs [?] … great compunction, one can see [?] … to tear down the whole dividing wall, remove the obstacle, and shorten the length of the road. For "I am a God near at hand," he says, "and not a God far off"; and, "The Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth." But now many of the faithful have gone so far in folly and contempt that, though full of countless evils and taking no care of themselves at all, they come to this table carelessly and casually at the feasts. They do not know that the time for communion is not a feast or a festival, but a pure conscience and a life free of charges against it. Just as someone conscious of no wrongdoing ought to come every day, so for someone caught up in sins and not repenting it is not safe to come even at a feast. Coming once a year does not free us from the charges against us if we come unworthily; rather, this very thing condemns us more, that coming only once, we do not come with purity even then. That is why I urge you all not to touch the divine mysteries simply because the feast demands it. If you are going to share in this holy offering, purify yourselves many days beforehand through repentance, prayer, almsgiving and attention to spiritual things, and do not then go back like a dog to its own vomit. Is it not absurd to take so much care over bodily things that when a feast comes round, many days in advance you take your finest garment out of the chests and get it ready, buy shoes, keep a more lavish table, devise many means from every quarter, and brighten and adorn yourself in every way, while you take no account of your soul, neglected, filthy, squalid, wasting away from hunger and remaining unclean, but bring the body here adorned and leave the soul naked and disgraceful? Yet it is a fellow servant who sees the body, and no harm at all comes even if [?] …

[Some manuscripts read: "to approach this table, not knowing." Others: "to the one who did evil, so much."]

To those who were absent from the assembly; a proof that the Son is consubstantial with the Father; and that the lowly things said and done by him were done and said not because of weakness of power or inferiority, but for various purposes of the divine dispensation. Following the discourses on the incomprehensible, and

Seventh Discourse.

1. Horse races again, and again our assembly has grown smaller. Or rather, as long as you are present, it could not grow smaller. A farmer who sees his wheat at its peak and fully ripe takes little account of the leaves that fall; so I too now, since the fruit is here with us, do not grieve so much over the leaves being snatched away …

[Savile reads: "various, and against the Anomoeans." Several manuscripts read: "being blown about."]

…I will try, by God's grace, to lead your love to the familiar meadow and the sea of the divine Scriptures. But rouse yourselves and stay awake. Among sailors, even if everyone sleeps while the helmsman alone stays awake, there is no danger; his watchfulness and skill suffice for the ship in place of everyone. Here it is not so. Even if the speaker is watchful ten thousand times over, if the listeners do not show the same wakefulness, our word will be swamped and lost, finding no mind to receive it. That is why we must be watchful and awake. Our trade is in greater goods: we do not sail for gold and silver and things that perish, but for the life to come and the treasures in heaven. The routes here are more numerous than those at sea or on land, and anyone who does not know how to steer them precisely will suffer the most grievous shipwreck. So all of you who sail with us, show not the carelessness of passengers but the wakefulness and concern of helmsmen. While all the rest sleep, they sit at the tillers, and not only watch the routes on the waters but look up to heaven across so vast a distance and, as if the course of the stars led them by the hand, steer the vessel safely. No layman could sail the sea by day as fearlessly as they do in all calm in the middle of the night, when the sea seems more terrifying; awake, they display their skill undisturbed, and watch not only the paths on the waters and the courses of the stars but also where the winds are coming from. So great is the wisdom of these men that often, when a gust of wind strikes more violently and is about to capsize the ship, they meet it skillfully by frequent shifts of the sails and dispel all the danger, and by setting their skill against the violent onslaughts of the winds they snatch the vessel from the surge. If they, sailing a visible sea for the affairs of this life, keep their souls so constantly awake, we must be prepared in this way much more. For the danger is greater for us if we are careless, and the safety greater if we are watchful. This vessel of ours is not built of planks; it is joined together from the divine Scriptures. No stars guide it from above; the Sun of righteousness directs this voyage for us. And we sit at the tillers awaiting not the breath of the west wind but the gentle breeze of the Spirit.

2. Let us be watchful, then, and survey the routes carefully, for our discourse is once more about the glory of the Only-begotten. The other day we showed that the comprehension of God's essence surpasses by a wide margin the wisdom of men, angels, archangels, and indeed all creation, and that it is known and clear to the Only-begotten alone and to the Holy Spirit. Now our discourse [moves on] to another part of the contest, by God's grace.

…a true son. And because of the title "god," since he shared that name with you, you will perhaps argue that the Father has nothing more than you; for just as you were called son, so you were also called god. But just as you, though called god, do not dare to say that in his case the name is a bare name, but confess that the Father is true God, so in the case of the Son do not dare to put yourself forward and say, "I too have been called son, and since I am not of the same essence, neither must he be of the same essence." For everything we have listed shows that he is a true Son and of the same essence as the one who begot him. When Scripture says that he is of the same form and the same exact imprint, what else does that show than that his essence is identical? For there is no form or face where God is concerned. "But since you say these things," he says, "speak also of the things that point the other way." What things? For example, that he prays to the Father. "If he is of the same power and the same essence and does all things by his own authority, why does he pray?"

3. I will speak not only of these things; I will set out carefully all the other lowly things that are said of him as well. But first I will say this: I can give many just reasons for the lowly things said of him, but you could give no other explanation for the lofty and glorious things than that he wishes to show us his own nobility. If that were not so, there would be conflict and war in the Scriptures. To say, "As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills," and all the other things I mentioned, and then to pray when there is need, would be contradictory. But once I give the reasons, all dispute is removed. What, then, are the reasons why both he and the apostles said many lowly things about him? The first and greatest reason is that he had clothed himself with flesh and wished to assure both the people of that time and all who came after that what was seen was not a shadow or a mere appearance but a true nature. For even though he and the apostles said so many lowly and human things about him, and he about himself, the devil still managed to persuade some wretched and miserable people to deny the doctrine of the incarnation, to dare to say that he did not take flesh, and to abolish the whole basis of his love for mankind. If he had said none of these things, how many would not have fallen into this pit? Do you not hear even now Marcion denying the incarnation, and Mani, and Valentinus, and many others? That is why he says many human and lowly things that fall short of that ineffable essence: to confirm the doctrine of the incarnation. For the devil has been very eager to remove this faith from people, knowing that if he removes faith in the incarnation, most of what concerns us will be lost. There is another reason after this one: the weakness of the hearers, and the fact that, seeing him then for the first time and hearing him then for the first time, they could not receive the loftier teachings of doctrine. And to show that what I say is not guesswork, I will try to prove it to you from the Scriptures themselves.

[Some manuscripts read: "this one into men."]

…[just as I have shown them] scandalized, troubled, leaping away, reviling him and fleeing whenever Christ said something great and lofty, so I will try to show them to you running to him and accepting his teaching whenever he said something lowly and humble. For they, the very same people who leapt away, ran to him at once when he said again, "I do nothing of myself, but I speak as my Father taught me." And the Evangelist, wishing to show us that they believed because of the lowliness of the words, points it out, saying, "As he said these things, many believed in him." One could find this happening in many other places as well. That is why he often spoke in a human way, and then again not in a human way but in a way befitting God and worthy of his own nobility: on the one hand condescending to the weakness of his hearers, on the other providing for the correctness of doctrine. For lest condescension, if it were constant, should harm those who came later in their opinion of his dignity, he did not neglect that side either. Although he knew beforehand that they would not listen but would revile him and [?] him, he spoke nonetheless, both establishing the very point I made and showing the reason why he mixed lowly words in with the rest. The reason was that they could not yet receive the greatness of what was said. If he had not wished to establish this, teaching lofty doctrines to people who would neither listen nor pay attention would have been pointless. But as it is, even if it did them no good, it taught us, prepared us to hold the right opinion about him, and persuaded us that he brought his discourse down to a lower level because they could not yet receive the greatness of what was said. So when you see him saying lowly things, consider that the condescension is due not to any inferiority in his essence but to the weakness in his hearers' understanding. Do you want me to give a third reason as well? Not only because he was clothed in flesh, and not only because of the weakness of his hearers, but also because he wished to teach his hearers humility, he did and said many lowly things; and this is a third reason. One who teaches humility teaches it not only by words but by deeds, showing modesty in word and in action. "Learn from me," he says, "for I am gentle and lowly in heart"; and again elsewhere, "The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve." So he who teaches us to become humble, never to rush after the first places but to accept being lesser everywhere, and who leads us to this by both words and deeds, had many reasons for speaking of lowly things. One may also give a fourth reason, no less important than those already given. What is it? That because of the great closeness and ineffable [?] of the hypostases we should never fall into the notion of a single person. Even now, though he said such things only rarely, some have already slipped into this impiety. Sabellius the Libyan, for instance, hearing him say, "I and the Father are one," and "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father," [took] the closeness to the one who begot him shown in these words as a basis for impiety…

[Some manuscripts read: "of what was said. But if … this." Others read: "is shown."]

…that Judas would betray him. He did it this way so that open reproof would not make Judas more shameless. But when Judas, stung by his conscience, said, "Is it I, Lord?" he said to him, "You have said it." Even then he could not bring himself to accuse him; instead he made Judas his own accuser. Yet not even so did Judas become better: he took the morsel and went out. Once he had gone out, Jesus took the disciples and said, "All of you will fall away because of me." Peter contradicted him, saying, "Even if all fall away, I will never fall away." Again Jesus said, "Truly I tell you, before the cock crows you will deny me three times." When Peter contradicted him again, he let him be from then on. "You are not persuaded by words," he means, "and you contradict me; you will be persuaded by the events themselves that one must not contradict the Master." Keep these words in mind for me, for remembering them will be useful to us when we examine the prayer. He named the traitor. He foretold the flight of them all, and his own death: "I will strike the shepherd," he says, "and the sheep will be scattered." He foretold who would deny him, and when, and how many times, all of it precisely. After all this, having given sufficient proof that he foreknew what was to come, he went to a certain place and prayed. They say that the prayer belongs to the Godhead; we say that it belongs to the economy of the incarnation. Judge, then, and for the sake of the glory of the Only-begotten, cast your vote as a favour to no one. Even though I am now pleading my case among friends, I beg and beseech you to make your judgment impartial, neither to please me nor out of hostility to them. Indeed it is clear at once that the prayer does not belong to the Godhead. God does not pray. It belongs to God to be worshipped; it belongs to God to receive prayer, not to offer it. Still, since they are shameless, I will try to show you from the very words of the prayer that the whole of it belongs to the economy and to the weakness of the flesh. Whenever Christ says something lowly, he says something so lowly and humble that the sheer lowliness of the words can persuade even the most contentious that they fall far short of that ineffable and inexpressible essence. Let us go, then, to the words of the prayer themselves: "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; yet not as I will, but as you will." Here let us ask them: does he not know whether it is possible or not? This is the one who said a little earlier at supper, "One of you will betray me"; who said a little earlier, "It is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered," and "All of you will fall away because of me"; who said to Peter, "You will deny me," and "You will deny me three times." Does he not know now, tell me? Who would say this, even among the most ordinary people? If the thing he did not know were clear to no one, not to prophets, angels or archangels, it might perhaps give the contentious some handle. But when the thing he supposedly did not know is so plain and familiar to everyone that even human beings know it precisely, what defence and what pardon is there for those who say that he spoke these words in ignorance? This one, then, of whom I speak, [Variant: others read ἀποδεῖται.]

we find in many places both foretelling the passion and desiring that it should happen, and having come for this very purpose. How then does he say here, "If it is possible"? He is showing us the weakness of human nature. That nature does not readily choose to be torn away from the present life; it shrinks back and hesitates, because of the love for the present life that God implanted in it from the beginning. He said so many great things, and still some dared to say that he did not take on flesh. If none of these things had been said, what would they not have said [?]? This is why there he foretells the passion as God and desires it to happen, while here he flees and begs to be spared as man. That he came to the passion willingly he shows when he says, "I have authority to lay down my life, and I have authority to take it up again. No one takes it from me; I lay it down of myself." How then does he say, "Not as I will, but as you will"? Why are you surprised that before the cross he took such pains to confirm the reality of his flesh? Even after the resurrection, when he saw his disciple disbelieving, he did not refuse to show him the wounds and the marks of the nails, to let him put his hand to the scars, and to say, "Search and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones" [?]. This is also why he did not take on manhood at full age from the beginning. He submitted to being conceived, born and nursed with milk, and to spending so long a time on earth, so that by the length of time and by everything else he might confirm this very thing. Angels often appeared on earth in human form, and so did God himself, but what appeared was not real flesh; it was condescension. So that you would not think this coming was like those, but would be truly assured that this was real flesh, he was conceived, born and nourished, and laid in a manger. This was not in some little house but in an inn, with a vast crowd present, so that his birth would be made public. This is also why there were swaddling clothes, and prophecies from long before saying this very thing: not only that he would be a man, but that he would be conceived, born and nourished in the manner of infants. Isaiah cries it out, saying: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel; butter and honey he shall eat." And again: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us." Do you see how they proclaimed even his early childhood in advance? So ask the heretic: does God fear, shrink back, hesitate and grieve? If he says yes, stand away from him from then on, and set him down below with the devil, or rather lower still, for not even the devil would dare to say this. But if he says that none of these things is worthy of God, say: "Then God does not pray either." Besides this, another absurdity follows if the words are God's. The words reveal not only agony but also two wills opposed to each other, one of the Son and one of the Father; for saying "Not as I will, but as you will" is what someone revealing this would say. Yet this they never conceded. Whenever we cite "I and the Father are one" with reference to power, they apply it to the will… [Variant: some MSS read ἐποιήσατο.] [Variant: some MSS read τὴν βαφήν, ἐπειδὰν δὲ πολλάκις.]

…of those who pray would come about. Consider how great a thing it will be. Angels are present, archangels stand by, the Seraphim, the Cherubim and all the other powers, and yet a human being can approach with great boldness and converse with the King of those powers. What honour would this not be worth? Not honour only, but also the greatest benefit comes to us from prayer, even before we receive what we ask for. As soon as someone raises his hands to heaven and calls on God, he immediately withdraws from all human affairs and is carried in mind to the life to come. From then on he pictures the things in heaven and has nothing to do with the present life for the time of his prayer, if he prays attentively. Even if anger is boiling up, it is easily lulled to sleep; if desire is burning, it is quenched; if envy is consuming him, it is driven out with great ease. What the prophet says happens at sunrise takes place. What does he say? "You made darkness, and it became night; in it all the beasts of the forest roam, young lions roaring to snatch their prey and to seek their food from God. The sun rose, and they gathered together, and they will lie down in their dens." When the sun's ray rises, all the beasts are put to flight and slink back into their lairs. In the same way, when prayer shines out from our mouth and tongue like a ray of light, the mind is enlightened, and all the irrational and beastly passions run off, are put to flight and slink back into their own lairs, provided only that we pray attentively, with a wakeful soul and a sober mind. Then, even if the devil is present, he is put to flight; even if a demon is there, it withdraws. When a servant is talking with his master, none of his fellow servants, not even one who has freedom to speak, would dare to come up and bother him. Much less could these beings, who have offended and have no boldness, bother us while we are conversing with God with the [Variant: others read "to God"]

[?] honour due to him. [Variant: Savile and others read ἐφθέγξατο; Morel reads ἐφθέγγετο.]

On the remaining points against the heretics, on judgment and almsgiving, and on the request of the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Eighth Discourse.

1. Yesterday we came back from war, from war and battle with the heretics. Our weapons were stained with blood and the sword of the word was reddened, though we had struck down no bodies. We had destroyed reasonings and "every lofty thing raised up against the knowledge of God." That is the form this battle takes, and so the weapons are of the same nature. Blessed Paul taught us both when he said: "For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful for God" [Variant: others, among them Savile, read the title as "By the same author, against the heretics, and on the request of the sons of Zebedee."] [?] ἐκείνη. [Variant: some MSS and Morel read τοῦ Χριστοῦ.]

…to slip away from what was said. Those matters you will learn from them. What must be said today we will tell you ourselves, setting out the objection that the children of the heretics brought against us. What is it? The other day we were discussing the authority of the Only-begotten and showing that his authority is equal to that of the Father who begot him, and we spent a long discourse on this. Stung by what was said, they brought against us a saying from the Gospel, one spoken in one sense but taken by them in another. "And yet it is written," they said, "'But to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give; it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.'" What I always urge on your love, I urge and counsel today too: do not simply skim the letters, but search out the meanings. Whoever simply sits by the words and looks for nothing beyond what is written will make many errors. The letters say that God has wings, for the prophet says, "In the shelter of your wings you will shelter me." But we will not therefore say that that spiritual and imperishable essence has wings. If this cannot be said even of human beings, much less can it be said of that pure, invisible and incomprehensible nature. What then are we to understand by the wings? His help, protection, shelter and alliance, the invincibility of his help. Again, the Scriptures say that he sleeps: "Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord?" This is not so that we should suppose God sleeps, which would be the height of folly. The word "sleep" shows us his long-suffering and forbearance. Yet another prophet says, "Is he like a man who sleeps?" Do you see how much understanding we need as we search the treasure of the divine Scriptures? If we listen to what is said simply, carelessly and at random, not only will those absurdities follow, but much conflict will also appear among the sayings. One says he sleeps and another that he does not. Yet both are true if you take them in the proper sense. The one who says he sleeps shows the intensity of his long-suffering; the one who says he does not sleep shows us the purity of his nature. Since we need much understanding, then, let us not take this saying simply either: "It is not mine to give; it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father." It does not take away his authority or cut short his sovereignty. It proves his great care, wisdom and providence for our race. To see that he is lord both to punish and to honour, hear what the very one who says these things says: "When the Son of Man comes in the glory of his Father, he will set the sheep at his right and the goats at his left. He will say to those at his right, 'Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink.' And to those at his left he will say, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not…'" [?] [Variant: Savile reads "the Scriptures, as in 'Arise.'"] [?] [Variant: soon after, τὸ αἰώνιον after τὸ πῦρ.] [?]

Are you poor, poorer than anyone? Still, you are not poorer than that widow who outdid the rich, though they gave out of great abundance. [?] Do you lack the food you need? Still, you are not more destitute than the woman of Sidon. [?] let us bring into the midst the best of all people and show him crowned by him; what excuse will be left to you then? [?] She had come to the very bottom of famine and was expecting death at any moment, with a band of children standing around her. Even so she did not spare what she had. Through her extreme poverty she bought unspeakable wealth: she made her hand a threshing floor and her jar a winepress, and caused much to spring from little. But let us go back to our subject, so as not to keep digressing. When the bridegroom was about to come, the virgins said these things to one another. The wise ones sent the others to the sellers, but it was no longer the time to buy oil, and rightly so. The sellers exist only in the present life. After our departure from here, when the theatre has closed, no remedy can be found any longer for what has been done, nor pardon nor excuse; punishment is inevitable from then on. That is what happened then too. When the bridegroom came, some went in with their lamps shining. The others, too late to go in, knocked on the doors of the bridal chamber and heard that fearful word: "Go away, I do not know you." Did you see him again both honouring and punishing, crowning and chastising, receiving and sending away, lord of both sides of the judgment? One can see this also in the case of the vineyard, and of the five talents, the two talents and the one. Some he accepted and set over more; the other he ordered to be bound and thrown outside into the outer darkness.

2. But what is their clever argument, or rather their argument full of great folly? They say he has authority to punish and to crown, to chastise and to reward, but that the highest precedence and the loftiest honour, he said, is not his to give. Then if you learn that nothing is exempt from his verdict, will you ever lay aside this misplaced contentiousness? Listen to him again: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son." If he has all judgment, nothing is exempt from his verdict, for whoever has all judgment is lord to chastise and to crown everyone. But do not hear "has given" here in a human way, beloved. He did not give to one who lacked it. He did not beget him imperfect, and nothing was added to him later. "Gave" means this: he begot him as such, perfect and complete. He uses this word so that you will not think there are two unbegotten gods, but will know both the root and the fruit, and not so that you will think this was added to him later. When he was asked elsewhere, "So you are a king?", he did not say, "I received the kingdom," or that the kingdom was added to him later. He said, "For this I was born." If he was born a complete king, he is clearly also judge and arbiter, for of a king… [Variant: one MS reads ἐπανίωμεν.] [Variant: πολύς used to be read; but δριμύς [?]] [?] θοῦσθαι τὸν οἰκεῖον, but here I need more [?] [Variant: others read τί οὖν ἐστιν ὃ αὐτὸν στεφανοῖ.]

…of zeal, so as not to overlook the part that limps or pass by anyone who is troubled. Here is what I say, but do not be troubled or disturbed by it: I say it is not the Son's to give, and not the Father's either. I proclaim this with a loud voice, clearer than a trumpet: it is not his to give, neither his nor the Father's. If it were his, it would be the Father's too; if it were the Father's, it would be his too. That is why he did not simply say, "It is not mine to give." What did he say? "It is not mine to give; it is for those for whom it has been prepared." He shows that it belongs neither to him nor to the Father, but to certain others. What then does the saying mean? I think your confusion has increased, your perplexity has grown and you are anxious. But do not be afraid: I will not stop until I have given you the solution. Bear with me a little while I take the discourse further back, for there is no other way to set everything clearly before your minds. What then does the saying mean? As Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, the mother of the sons of Zebedee, James and John, came to him with her sons and said, "Say that my two sons may sit, one at your right and one at your left." Another evangelist says that the sons themselves asked this of Christ. But there is no disagreement (we must not pass over even such small points). They put their mother forward, and since she spoke and opened the door, they too presented the petition. They did not know what they were saying, yet they said it. Though they were apostles, they were still rather imperfect, like nestlings fluttering about in the nest before their wings have grown firm. You especially need to know this: before the cross they were in great ignorance. That is why he rebuked them, saying: "Are you also still without understanding? Do you not yet perceive or understand that it was not about bread that I told you to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees?" And again: "I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now." Not only were they ignorant of the higher things; they often lost what they did hear, out of fear and cowardice. He reproached them for this, saying: "None of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart." And again, speaking of the Paraclete: "He will remind you of all things and teach you." He would not have said "remind" unless they had let slip much of what had been said. I have not said all this idly. I said it because Peter appears at one moment making a perfect confession and at another having forgotten everything. The one who said, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God," and was called blessed for it, sinned so badly shortly afterwards that he was called Satan. For he says, "Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, for you are not minding the things of God, but the things of men." What could be more imperfect than someone who does not mind God's things but the things of men? Christ had been speaking with him about the cross and the resurrection, and Peter did not know the depth of what was said, nor the mystery of the doctrines, nor the salvation that was about to come upon the world. [Variant: some MSS and Savile read "but of the Father, what" [?]] [?] [Variant: one Royal MS reads προϐαλλόμενος.] [Variant: one MS has πλαττόμενοι; Savile has πλαζόμενοι.] [Variant: four MSS read καὶ ταῦτα μάλιστα.] [The words "What could be more imperfect… of men" are not found in Savile.] [?] [Variant: Savile reads στοχασμός and πιθανότητες [?]; Montfaucon πιθανότης [?].]

…of those who are lost. You have not yet sprung from the starting line; you have not yet stripped for the bouts. “Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink, and to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” Here he calls his own cross and death a cup and a baptism. He calls it a cup because he went to it gladly, and a baptism because through it he cleansed the world. That is not the only reason, though; it is also because of the ease of the resurrection. Someone baptized in water comes up again with great ease, not hindered at all by the nature of the water. In the same way he went down into death and came up with still greater ease, and that is why he calls it a baptism. What he means is this: “Are you able to be slaughtered and to die? For now is the time for these things: for deaths, dangers and toils.” They say, “We are able.” They did not even know what was being said, but they made the promise in the hope of getting what they had asked for. He says to them, “You will drink the cup, and you will be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized.” By this he means death, for James was beheaded with the sword, and John died many times over. “But to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give; it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared.” What he means is this: “You will die, you will be slaughtered, and you will be honored with martyrdom. But to become first is not mine to give. It is for those who compete to win it, by greater zeal and greater eagerness.” To make my meaning clearer, let us suppose there is a president of the games. Then suppose a mother whose two sons are athletes comes with her sons to the president and says, “Promise that these two sons of mine will receive the crown.” What will he answer? Exactly this: “It is not mine to give. I am the president of the games. I award the prizes not by favor, nor because of the pleading and entreaty of those who come to me, but by the outcome of the contest.” For this above all belongs to a president of the games: not to hand out the prizes at random, as chance falls, but to honor courage. This is just what Christ does. He did not speak this way to set aside what belongs to his own being. He wanted to show that it is not his alone to give; it is also up to those who compete to win. If it were his alone, all people would have been saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. If it were his alone, there would be no differences of honor, for he made everyone and cares for everyone alike. That there are different honors, hear Paul showing it when he says, “There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.” And again: “If anyone builds on this foundation gold, silver, precious stones.” Paul framed his words this way to show how varied virtue is. He said these things to show that we cannot enter the kingdom of heaven while sleeping and snoring; those prizes must be won through many tribulations. For since they enjoyed great friendship and freedom of speech with him, they thought that they would take precedence [?] even over the others… [Editorial notes:] “went to it”: correct. Two [manuscripts] read “held fast.” Savile and one [manuscript] read τιμῶντα, others τιμῶντος. [?] “showing it and.”

…to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. “You can see from what happened in my own case,” he says, “that this is what makes people illustrious and distinguished. I have no need of honor or glory, and yet through this I too accomplish countless good things.” Before he took flesh and humbled himself, everything had perished and been ruined. But when he humbled himself, he raised everything up [?: a garbled phrase, “…of the many you pursue, and the service”]. He abolished the curse, quenched death, opened paradise and put sin to death. He threw open the vaults of heaven and carried our firstfruits up to heaven. He filled the world with godliness, drove out error and brought back the truth. He made our firstfruits ascend the royal throne. He worked countless good things which neither I nor all humankind could ever describe in words. Before he humbled himself, only the angels knew him; but when he humbled himself, the whole of human nature came to know him. See how his humility brought about no diminishment, but countless gains and countless achievements, and made his glory shine out all the more. But if in the case of God, who lacks nothing and needs nothing… [?] …you will be exalted. [Editorial note: for which (one manuscript) has] “with great zeal.”

On Lazarus, Four Days Dead. Homily Nine.

1. Today Lazarus, raised from the dead, gives us the answer to many different stumbling blocks. Somehow this reading has given the heretics a handle and the Jews an excuse for argument. This comes not from the truth, God forbid, but from their own malicious souls. Many of the heretics say that the Son is not like the Father. Why? “Because,” they say, “Christ needed prayer to raise Lazarus. If he had not prayed, he would not have raised Lazarus. And how,” they say, “can the one who prayed be like the one who received the plea? One prays; the other received the prayer from the one pleading.” They blaspheme, because they do not understand that the prayer was an act of condescension, made on account of the weakness of those present. Tell me: who is greater, the one who washes feet or the one whose feet are washed? Surely the one whose feet are washed is greater than the one washing them. Yet the Savior washed the feet of Judas the traitor, for he was with the disciples. Is Judas the traitor, then, greater than Christ the Master, since Christ washed his feet? God forbid! And which is lowlier, to wash feet or to pray? Surely to wash feet. Then if he did not refuse to do the lowlier thing, how would he have refused to do the loftier one? But everything for… [?] [Editorial note: some read “harm” for “handle.”]

…call that ignorance too. Take another proof from the divine Scripture. God said to Abraham, “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has come to me. I will go down, then, and see whether they have done according to the outcry that comes to me; and if not, that I may know.” God knows all things before they come to be. He tests hearts and minds, and he alone knows the thoughts of human beings. Yet he said, “I will go down, then, and see whether they have done according to the outcry that comes to me; and if not, that I may know.” If that was ignorance, then this too is ignorance. But neither was the Father ignorant in the Old Testament, nor the Son in the New. What, then, does this mean: “I will go down and see whether they have done according to the outcry that comes to me; and if not, that I may know”? “A report,” he says, “has come to me. But I want to test it more exactly through the facts themselves. This is not because I am ignorant, but because I want to teach people not simply to pay attention to words. If someone says something against another person, they should not believe it readily. They should first examine it carefully and learn by putting it to the test through the facts themselves, and only then believe.” That is why he said in another Scripture, “Do not believe every word.” Nothing so overturns human life as believing reports quickly. The prophet David said this too, in prophecy: “Him who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I [drove out]…”

2. You have seen that there was no ignorance in the Savior when he said, “Where have you laid him?”, just as there was none in the Father when he said to Adam, “Where are you?”, or to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?”, or, “I will go down and see whether they have done according to the outcry that comes to me; and if not, that I may know.” So now it is time to draw up for battle against those who say that Christ raised Lazarus by praying because he was weak. Pay attention, beloved, with all care, I beg you. Lazarus died. Jesus was not in that region but in Galilee, and he said to his disciples, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep.” They thought he was speaking of ordinary sleep, and said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.” Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus is dead.” Then the Savior comes to Jerusalem, to the place where Lazarus lay. Lazarus’s sister meets him and says to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” “If you had been here”! You are weak, woman. The woman does not yet understand that even when Christ was not present in body, he was present by the authority of his divinity. She measures the Teacher’s power by his bodily presence. Martha says to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. And even now,” she says, “I know that whatever you ask of God, he gives you.” So the Savior offers the prayer in response to her request. God did not need prayer to raise the dead. Did he not raise other dead people too? When he met a dead man being carried out at the town gate, he merely touched the bier and raised the dead man. Did he need prayer then to raise the dead man? And again, at another time, he simply spoke a word…

…is mine, and that is my Father’s. For I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.

3. So that you may see that the rising of the dead man was not the work of prayer, listen to the prayer itself. What does he say? “I thank you, Father, that you have heard me.” What then? Is this the form of a prayer? Is this the pattern of a plea? “I thank you that you have heard me.” “I knew,” he says, “that you always hear me.” If you know, O Lord, that the Father always hears you, why trouble him about what you already know? “I know,” he says, “that the Father always hears me. But I said this because of the crowd standing around, so that all may know that you sent me.” Did he pray for the dead man? Did he plead that Lazarus might rise? Did he say, “Father, command death to obey”? Did he say, “Father, command Hades not to keep its gates shut, but to give up the dead man willingly”? No. “I said this because of this crowd standing around,” he says, “so that all may know that you sent me.” So the prayer was not what performed the sign; it was instruction for those present. You have seen that the prayer was not made for the dead man but for the unbelievers who were there: “so that they may know,” he says, “that you sent me.” “And how are we to know,” someone says, “that he sent you?” Pay attention, I beg you, with all care. “Look,” he says, “by my own authority I call the dead man. Look, by my own power I give orders to death. I call the Father ‘Father,’ and I call Lazarus out of the tomb. If the first is not true, let the second not happen either. But if the Father is truly Father, let the dead man obey too, for the instruction of those present.” For what did Christ say? “Lazarus, come out!” When the prayer was made, the dead man did not rise; but when he said, “Lazarus, come out!”, then the dead man rose. O tyranny of death! O tyranny of that power which held the soul fast! O Hades, a prayer has been made, and you do not release the dead man? “No,” it says. Why? “Because I was not commanded. I am a prisoner here, holding the one who is liable [?]…” […] …they slander the thing as an apparition.

That not to speak what we know and bring it out to others makes us poorer and quenches grace. Also on the prayers that Christ prayed, and the authority with which he did all things; on the correction of the old law; and that becoming flesh does not diminish his equality with the Father, but rather confirms it.

Homily Ten.

1. We have celebrated fully on the preceding days. We took up the contests of the apostles and delighted in the story of their spiritual achievements. Now it is time to pay you what I owe, for nothing stands in the way. I know that you have forgotten my debts to you because there have been so many parts [?]. Even so, I will not hide them; I will pay them to you with all eagerness. I do this not only out of fairness but also for my own benefit. In bodily transactions the borrower gains when the lender forgets; but in spiritual ones…

…[if I] bring it out, and make many people sharers and partners in everything I myself know, my spiritual wealth increases. That this is so is shown by those who were entrusted with the talents: the one with five, the one with two, and the one with one. Whoever shares with others increases what was entrusted to him, while whoever hides it shrinks the whole enterprise. The first two brought back double what had been entrusted to them, and were honored for it. The last kept it to himself and shared it with no one, so he could not double it, and he was punished for it. So let all of us hear this and fear the punishment that comes from there. Let us bring out to our brothers whatever good we have and lay it out openly for everyone, and not hide it. When we share with others, we ourselves grow richer. When we take many partners into our trade, we increase our own wealth. But you think your glory is diminished when many others know what you alone know. On the contrary, both your glory and your benefit increase when you trample on envy, when you quench jealousy, when you show great love for your brothers. But if you go about as the only one who knows, people will turn away from you and hate you as jealous and a hater of your brothers, and God will exact from you the utmost penalty as a wicked man. Besides this, grace itself will quickly leave you and abandon you, desolate. Take grain, too. If it lies in the storehouses all the time, it is wasted as the weevil eats it; but if it is brought out and sown in the fields, it multiplies and is renewed. So too with a spiritual word. If it is always shut up inside, it is quickly snuffed out, because the soul is corrupted and eaten away by envy, sloth and decay. But if it is sown in the souls of the brothers as in fertile ground, the treasure multiplies, both for those who receive it and for the one who has it. Again, a spring that is constantly drawn from is cleansed all the more and gushes out more abundantly, but when it is filled in, it is choked. In the same way a spiritual gift and a word of teaching gush out more abundantly when they are constantly drawn upon and let those who wish draw from them. But when they are buried under jealousy and envy, they dwindle and are completely snuffed out. Since we gain so much, come, let us lay out openly whatever we have and pay you the whole debt. But first let me remind you of the whole sequence of these debts.

2. You know and remember that the other day, when we were discussing the glory of the Only-begotten, we listed many reasons for the condescension in his words. We said that Christ often speaks humbly not only because he was clothed in flesh, nor only because his hearers were weak, but in many places also to teach humility. We dealt fully with those reasons then. We mentioned both the prayer at Lazarus’s tomb and the one made at the cross itself, and showed clearly that he made the first to confirm the truth of his incarnation and the second to correct the weakness of his hearers, while he himself needed no help. That he did many things to teach them humility as well, hear this too. He poured water into the basin; and as if not…

…you would see him doing and saying things somewhere [?]. In the same way he offers many of his prayers with the same intention. For they came to him saying, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” What should he have done, tell me? Not teach them to pray? But he came precisely to lead them into the whole of true wisdom. So he had to teach them? Then [he had] to pray…

“But he should have done this by word alone,” someone says. Teaching by words, however, does not usually lead learners on as teaching by deeds does. That is why he does not only teach them prayer in words, but keeps doing it himself, and prays all night in lonely places. He is training and warning us that whenever we are about to converse with God, we should flee noise and the turmoil of the world and withdraw into solitude, a solitude not only of place but also of time. And solitude is not only a mountain; it can also be a little room free from clamor.

3. That this prayer is an act of condescension, we have already shown, above all from what happened in the case of Lazarus. But it is clear from elsewhere as well. Why does he not pray at the greater miracles, but at the lesser ones? If he prayed because he needed help and did not have power of his own, he ought to have prayed at all of them and called on the Father. If not at all of them, then at least at the greater ones. In fact he does the opposite. He does not pray over the greater deeds, to show that he prayed to train others, not because he needed power. When he blessed the loaves, for instance, he looked up to heaven and prayed. He was training us not to taste a meal until we have given thanks to God, who made the fruits of the earth. And though he raised many dead people, he did not pray, except over Lazarus alone. We gave the reason then: he was correcting the weakness of those present. He stated it himself, adding plainly, “I said this because of the crowd standing around.” We also showed fully then that it was not the prayer but his voice that raised the dead man. And so that you may learn this more clearly,

when he has to punish, or honor, or forgive sins, or give laws, or do any of the far greater things, you will nowhere find him calling on the Father or praying. You will find him doing everything with authority. I will list each of these; you, for your part, notice carefully that he nowhere needs prayer. “Come,” he says, “you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you.” And again: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” See, he punishes and honors with authority [?], and needs no prayer at all. Again, when a paralyzed body has to be restored: “Get up, take your bed and walk.” When [he has] to set free from death… [?]

…and a humbled [heart] God will not despise. And again: “Blessed are the meek.” Isaiah too cries this out, speaking in the person of God: “On whom shall I look, if not on the meek and quiet one who trembles at my words?” “Blessed are the merciful.” This too is scattered everywhere: “Do not defraud the poor of his livelihood,” it says, “do not turn away a suppliant in distress.” Everywhere there is much said about kindness. [551] “Blessed are the pure in heart.” David says this too: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.” If anyone goes through the remaining beatitudes, he will find a great deal of agreement. Why then, when he had said nothing contrary to the earlier teachings, did he add, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets”? He puts in this correction not because of what had already been said, but because of what was about to be said. He was about to go on to make the commandments stricter. So that they would not think the increase was opposition, or the addition a conflict, he said, “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets.” That is, “I am about to say some things more perfect than those said before.” For example: “You have heard, ‘You shall not murder’; but I say, ‘You shall not be angry.’ You have heard, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say that whoever looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery,” and so on. So do not think that perfecting is abolishing. It is not abolition but fulfillment, and what he did with bodies he does with the law as well. What did he do with bodies? He came and found many limbs maimed and everything defective, and he made them whole and restored them to their proper order. Through the deeds themselves he made it plain to everyone that he himself had laid down the ancient laws and had fashioned our nature. That he was eager to show this is clearest of all from the healing of the blind man. Passing by and seeing a blind man, he made clay, smeared that clay on the maimed eyes, and said to him, “Go, wash in Siloam.” Why, when he constantly raised the dead by a bare command and worked many other such wonders, does he add an action here, making clay and molding the eyes with it? Is it not evident? It was so that when you hear that God took dust from the earth and formed man, you might learn from what is done now that this is the one who formed man in the beginning. If he had not wished to show this, what he did would have been superfluous. Then, so that you might learn that it was not the use of the clay that helped him restore sight to the maimed man, and that a command alone was enough to form the eyes even without that material, he adds, “Go, wash in Siloam.” Only after showing us by the manner of the creation that he was the one who had also made man in the beginning does he say to him, “Go, wash in Siloam.” An excellent sculptor who wishes to display his art through his works leaves part of the statue unfinished as he molds it, so that in the missing part he may give proof of his skill over the whole. In the same way Christ, [to show] that he himself made the whole man [?]… Christ came, undertaking greater things, wishing to show [?]… he left this incomplete, so that coming [?]… to us. And consider with [?]…

…he reads out the old laws and sets the new ones beside them. “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not murder.’” Say also by whom it was said: did you say it, or the Father [?]? But he does not say. Why then did he keep silent about this? Why did he not make the speaker plain, but brought in the legislation without naming anyone? Suppose he had said, “[My Father said] ‘You shall not murder,’ [556] but I say to you, ‘You shall not be angry.’” The saying would have seemed harsh because of the folly of his hearers. They were not yet able to understand that he was legislating by enlarging the earlier laws, not by overturning them. They would have said to him, “What are you saying? Your Father said, ‘You shall not murder,’ and you say, ‘You shall not be angry’?” So that no one would think he was opposed to the Father, or was bringing in something more as if he were wiser than the Father, he did not say, “You have heard from the Father.” Again, if he had said, “You have heard that I said to the ancients,” it would have seemed intolerable, no less than the first way. When he said, “Before Abraham came to be, I am,” they tried to stone him. If he had added that he himself had also given Moses the law, what would they not have done? So he said nothing about himself or about the Father, but left it open and said, “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not murder.’” With bodies, by filling up what was lacking, he taught them that he was also the one who fashioned man in the beginning. He does the same here: by correcting the law and adding what was lacking, he teaches who it was that gave the law in the beginning as well. For this reason too, when he discussed the creation of man, he mentioned neither himself nor the Father. There too he spoke without naming anyone and left it undefined, saying, “He who made them from the beginning made them male and female.” In word he kept silent about the Maker, but in deed he taught it, by filling up what was lacking in bodies. So here too, when he said, “You have heard that it was said to the ancients,” he kept silent about who said it, but he revealed himself through the deeds themselves. The one who filled up what was lacking is the one who also brought in the law at the beginning. He reads out the old laws themselves so that his hearers might learn, by setting the two side by side, that his words are not in opposition and that he has the same authority as the one who begot him. The Jews too understood this, and they marveled. Hear the evangelist showing that they marveled: “The crowds,” he says, “were astonished at his teaching, for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes and the Pharisees.” “What then,” someone says, “if they were wrong to suspect this?” Yet he did not accuse them or rebuke them; he even confirmed their judgment. When the leper came up right afterward and said, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean,” what does he say? “I will; be clean.” Why did he not simply say, “Be clean”? The leper had already testified that he had authority by saying, “If you will.” But so that you would not think “if you will” was merely the leper's opinion, he added it himself, saying, “I will; be clean.” In this way he deliberately showed his own authority everywhere, and that… [Note: Savile conjectures that one should read: “he said, ‘My Father said to the ancients, “You shall not…”’”]

…but one who has a good that cannot be taken away is not afraid, even if he hides it. To make my point clear by an example, suppose someone has two [dependents], one a household slave and the other a son. If the slave lays claim to a freedom that in no way belongs to him and sets himself against his master, he will not bring himself to do anything servile [558] or obey when he is given orders. He is afraid that this very thing will damage his freedom and that the order will make him stumble, for he has seized the honor and holds it undeservedly. But the son will not refuse to do any servile task. He knows that even if he performs every one of the slaves' duties, his freedom suffers no harm but stays unshaken. Natural nobility cannot be taken away by servile work, because he does not hold it by seizure, as the slave does; it was his portion from the beginning, from his first day. Paul shows this about Christ when he says that, since Christ was free by nature and a true Son, he had not taken equality as a thing seized and so did not need to hide it, but confidently took the form of a slave. For he knew, he knew clearly, that his condescension could not diminish his glory in the least. That glory was not brought in from outside, not obtained by seizure, not foreign to him or unfitting, but natural and his own. That is why he took the form of a slave, knowing clearly and fully convinced that this could do him no harm. And indeed it did him no harm: even in the form of a slave he kept the same glory. Do you see that his very taking of flesh is a sign that the Son is equal to the one who begot him? It also shows that this equality was not brought in from outside, and does not come and go, but is unshaken and firm, the kind a son may be expected to have in relation to a father. 7. Let us then say all this to them, and strive, as far as it lies with us, to lead them away from that wicked heresy and bring them back to the truth. And let us ourselves not think that faith alone is enough for our salvation. Let us also take care how we live and show the best kind of life, so that what makes for our benefit may be complete on both sides. What I urged the other day I urge again now, so that you may carry it out: let us put an end to our enmities toward one another. Let no one remain his neighbor's enemy for more than a single day. Let him put an end to his anger before night falls. Otherwise, alone with his thoughts and carefully gathering up everything done and said during the quarrel, he will make the outcome harsher and the reconciliation more difficult. Think of the bones of our body when they are dislocated from their proper sockets. If they are put back at once, they regain their place without much pain. But if they stay out of their sockets for a long time, it is hard to get them back where they belong, and once they are set back they need many days to fit precisely, settle, and stay in place. It is the same with us. If we are reconciled with our enemies at once, we do it easily and need no great effort to return to our old friendship. But if much time passes in between, we are as if blinded by the enmity: we blush, we are ashamed, we need others [?]… to prevent those who are about to become…, and to make those of our friends who…

…are, safer. For indeed [?]… heaven [?]… by the grace and love for humanity [?]… which may we all [?]… [559?] [?]… continually enjoying [?]… the kingdom [?]… forever and ever. Amen. [561] HOMILY delivered in Constantinople against the Anomoeans, on the incomprehensible, that the New Testament agrees with the Old, and against those who stay away from the divine assemblies. Eleventh discourse. 1. I spoke to you on a single day, and from that day I have loved you as though I had been brought up with you from the beginning, from my first [day]. I was bound to you by the bonds of love as if I had enjoyed your most delightful company for a time beyond telling. This has happened not because I am an especially friendly and affectionate person, but because you, above all people, are dear and lovable. For who would not admire and marvel at your fiery zeal, your unfeigned love, [Notes: Others read: “Discourse [?] of the same, on the incomprehensible, against the Anomoeans.” Savile: “Against the Anomoeans, on the consubstantial.” [?] Savile: “Against the Anomoeans, on the consubstantial.” After [?] one manuscript also adds “and to take.” Others: “and much of the man[ly]…” [?]]

…is spent. Squall, storm and surging sea constantly surround this holy ship, and those sailing in it are not drowned. The assault of the heretical flame encircles it on every side, and those in the middle of the furnace enjoy a spiritual dew. To see this Church planted in this part of the city is as marvelous as seeing an olive tree flourishing in the middle of a furnace, covered in leaves and laden with fruit. You are so well disposed and worthy of countless blessings. So come, let us gladly pay you what we promised the other day, when we were discussing among you the weapons of David and Goliath. Our discourse showed that the one was fenced in on every side by a great and mighty suit of armor, while the other, stripped of that armor, was walled in by faith. The one gleamed outwardly with breastplate and shield; the other gleamed inwardly with the Spirit and grace. That is why the boy defeated the young man, the unarmed overcame the armed, and the shepherd threw down the soldier: the nature of a shepherd's stone crushed and destroyed the nature of bronze made for war. So let us too take up that stone. I mean the cornerstone, the spiritual one. If Paul may draw a spiritual lesson from the rock in the wilderness, surely no one will begrudge our taking this stone in the same way. With the Jews, it was not the nature of the visible rock that released those rivers of water, but the power of the rock understood spiritually. [542] So too with David, it was not the stone of the senses but the spiritual stone that brought down that barbarian head. That is why we promised you, then as well, that we would say nothing drawn from mere reasoning. “For our weapons are not fleshly but spiritual, tearing down reasonings and every height raised up against the knowledge of God.” We are commanded, then, to tear these down, not to exalt them; we have been ordered to overthrow them, not to arm ourselves with them. “For the reasonings of mortals are timid,” it says. What does “timid” mean? A timid man, even when he walks on safe ground, still has no confidence; he fears and trembles. In the same way, what is accepted on the strength of reasoning, even if it is true, does not yet give the soul full assurance and sufficient faith. Since reasoning is so weak, come, let us join battle with our opponents from the Scriptures. Where, then, should our discourse begin? Wherever you like, whether from the New Testament or from the Old. The glory of the Only-begotten shines out in great abundance not only in the words of the Gospels and the apostles, but also in the prophets and throughout the Old Testament. That is why I think it best to open my skirmish with them from there. By drawing our arguments from there we shall be able to overthrow not only these people but many other heretics as well: Marcion, Mani, Valentinus, and all the factions of the Jews. In David's case Goliath fell and the whole army fled. The death was of one body, and the blow fell on one head, but the flight and the panic were shared by the whole army. So too with us now: when one heresy is struck and falls, all those we have listed will flee together. [Notes: Others read “surrounding in a circle on every side,” and shortly after, “in the middle of the furnace.” Savile: “in the middle.” [?] “and great.” Below, others read “the other from within.” Others: “became of one body.” [?] both of these call the Son [?]…]

…his [counselor]? This one, then, showed that he has no need of anything. But Isaiah, speaking in turn about the Only-begotten of God, says something like this: “And they will wish that they had been burned with fire, for a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful Counselor.” And if he is a Wonderful Counselor, how can Paul say, “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” Because Paul, as I said before, wants to show that the Father has no need of anything, while the prophet wants to show that the Only-begotten is equal in honor. That is why here too he did not say, “Make,” but, “Let us make.” “Make” is a command given to a slave, and this is clear from the following. A centurion once came to Jesus and said, “Lord, my servant is lying at home paralyzed, in terrible torment.” What did Christ say? “I will come and heal him.” The centurion did not dare to drag the physician to his house, but the caring and loving Lord promised of his own accord to go there. He wanted to give the centurion an occasion and an opportunity to display his virtue to us. He knew what the centurion was about to say, and so he promised to come, so that you might learn the man's reverence. [544] For what does the centurion say? “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof.” Not even the pressure of the disease and the illness could make him forget his reverence; even in his misfortune he recognized the Master's superiority. That is why he says, “Only say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man with soldiers under me. I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” Do you see that “Do” is how a master speaks to a slave? So “Let us make” is how one speaks to an equal. When a master speaks to a slave, he says, “Do”; when the Father converses with the Son, he says, “Let us make.” “What then,” he says, “if the centurion supposed this, but the matter was not so? Is the centurion an apostle? Is he a disciple, that I should accept his words? He was likely mistaken,” he says. Very well. What then? Let us look at what follows. Did Christ correct him? Did he rebuke him as mistaken and as bringing in corrupt doctrines? Did he say to him, “What are you doing, man? You have a higher opinion of me than is fitting. You grant me more than is my due. You think I give orders with authority when I have no authority”? Did he say anything like this? Not at all. He even confirmed his judgment, and said to those who were following, “Truly I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such faith.” So the Master's praise becomes a confirmation of the centurion's words. The words spoken no longer belong to the centurion; they are the Master's verdict. When he himself praises what was said and gives his vote to it as well said, I receive it as a divine oracle, for it received its authority from above, from Christ's reply. 3. Do you see how the New Testament agrees with the Old? How each displays the authority of Christ? “What then,” [someone says], “if he did make man, but as an assistant [?]…” [Notes: [?] two [manuscripts] omit “from Christ's reply”; [?] “from the Lord's reply”; one has “from God's reply.” Others read “to sit, [?] of sovereign [?], extraordinary [?], but the…”]

…let [it] be preferred as a pastime. Tell me, what do you gain by staying away from the assembly that is as great as the loss you inflict on yourself and your whole household? Even if you found a whole treasure full of gold and missed the assembly because of it, your loss would be greater, and greater by as much as spiritual things are better than the things of the senses. However many those things may be, and even if they flow in from every side, they do not travel with us to the life there. They do not move with us to heaven or stand beside us at the fearful judgment seat. Often they leave us and are gone even before death. And even if they stay until the end, death certainly cuts them off. But the spiritual treasure is a possession that cannot be taken away. It follows us wherever we walk and wherever we travel, and it gives us great boldness before that judgment seat. [546] 4. If the gain from the other assemblies is so great, from the assemblies here it is doubled. We do not only reap the benefit of watering our soul with divine words. We also pour a great deal of shame on our enemies and give our brothers a great deal of encouragement. In a battle line, this is where the gain lies: in hurrying to the part of the fight that is hard pressed and full of danger. That is why everyone must come running here and drive back the enemies who are attacking. You cannot deliver a long speech? You have no teaching to give? Just be present, and you have done everything. The presence of your body adds to the flock, gives your brothers great eagerness, and covers your enemies with shame. If someone steps onto these sacred thresholds and sees only a few gathered, even the eagerness he has is quenched. He goes numb, shrinks back, grows more sluggish and withdraws. Then, little by little, our whole congregation becomes slacker and more careless. But if he sees people running together, eager, streaming in from every side, the zeal of the others becomes a source of eagerness even for someone very sluggish and listless. Stone rubbed against stone often makes sparks fly, and yet what is colder than stone, and what is hotter than fire? Still, persistence overcame nature. If this happens with stone, it happens much more with souls rubbing against one another and warmed by the fire of the Spirit. Have you not heard that in the time of our forefathers the believers numbered a hundred and twenty in all? Or rather, before the hundred and twenty there were only twelve. Not even all of these remained: one of them, Judas, perished, and they were eleven in all. Yet from those eleven came a hundred and twenty… [?] [Note: Others read “toward one another.”] [Homily] on the [paralytic] who had been thirty-eight years in his illness, and on the words “My Father is working until now” [?]… And yet we have not had many days since we sowed this seed, and look, a rich ear of obedience has already sprung up for us. This makes it clear that it is not human power but divine grace that tends this Church. For such indeed is the nature…

…of the spiritual sowing: it does not wait for time. It does not wait out a great number of days or look for the cycles of months, nor for hours and seasons and years. On a single day one can cast the seed and, with a full and laden arm, reap this harvest. Those who plough this visible earth need a great deal of labour and a long delay. They have to bring plough-oxen under the yoke, cut a deep furrow, sow the seed generously, level the surface of the ground, cover over everything sown, wait for rain in the right measure, toil at many other tasks and wait a long time, and only then do they reach the end. Here, though, one may sow and reap in summer and in winter alike, and often both have happened on the very same day, especially when the soul being farmed happens to be rich and fertile. This can be seen in your case, and that is why we run to you all the more eagerly. A farmer, too, works the field that suits him, the one from which he has often filled his threshing floor. Since you give us a large yield from little labour, we take up this farming with close attention, and we have come to bring you what remained of what we said before. Last time we wove our discourse on the glory of the only-begotten Son of God from the Old Testament; now we will do the same thing from it again. Then we said that Christ said, 'If you believed Moses, you would believe me.' Now we say that Moses said, 'The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; listen to him.' For just as Christ sends us on to Moses so as to draw us to himself through him, so Moses hands the disciples over to the teacher and bids them obey him in everything. Let us obey, then, whatever he does and says: in everything else, and in this sign that was read to us today. What is it? 'There was,' it says, 'a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now in Jerusalem, by the Sheep Gate, there is a pool, called in Hebrew Bethesda, which has five porticoes.' The story goes that an angel came at certain times and went down into it, and this was known from the stirring of the water. The first to step in after the water was disturbed was made well, whatever illness he had. 'In these porticoes, then, lay a crowd of sick people, blind, lame and withered, waiting for the stirring of the water.' Why, then, does Christ keep coming to Jerusalem and visiting the Jews at their feasts? Because the crowd gathered at those times, and he watched for that place and that moment so that he could lay hold of the sick. The sufferers did not want to be rid of their diseases as much as the physician was eager to rid them of their illness. So when their assembly was full and the theatre complete, he came into the middle of it and showed them what made for the salvation of their souls. A crowd of sick people, then, lay waiting for the stirring of the water, and the first to go down was healed after the…

…to bear what came upon him nobly and with all readiness. If it had been twenty years, or ten, or only five, would that not have been enough to break the strength of his soul? Yet he holds out for thirty-eight years, does not give up and shows great endurance. Perhaps the length of time strikes you as remarkable, but when you hear the words themselves, you will understand his wisdom and the full extent of his endurance. Jesus came up and said to him, 'Do you want to be made well?' Who would not know that he wanted to be made well? Why, then, does he ask? Not out of ignorance. He who knows the hidden things of the mind knew much better what was plain and clear to everyone. Why did he ask, then? On another occasion he said to the centurion, 'I will come and heal him.' He was not ignorant of what the man would say; he foresaw it and knew it precisely. He wanted to give him an opening and an occasion to reveal to all the piety that lay hidden in shadow, and to say, 'No, Lord, for I am not worthy that you should come under my roof.' In the same way, with this paralytic, he knew what the man would say and asks whether he wants to be healed. He asks not because he did not know, but to give him an occasion and a starting point to tell the full story of his misfortune, and so to become a teacher of endurance. If he had healed the man in silence, we would have suffered the greatest loss, for we would never have learned the fortitude of his soul. But Christ does not only set the present right; he takes great care for the future as well. So, by forcing him through his question to answer, he revealed him as a teacher of fortitude and endurance to everyone who lives in the world: 'Do you want to be made well?' What does the man do? He was not annoyed or indignant. He did not say to the one who asked, 'You can see I am paralysed. You know how long my illness has lasted, and you ask whether I want to be made well? Have you come to laugh at my misfortunes and make a comedy of other people's troubles?' You know how faint-hearted the sick become even if they lie in bed for just a year. When the illness had dragged on for thirty-eight years, would it not be likely that all his wisdom had been used up, spent over that long time? Yet he neither said nor thought anything of the kind. He answers with great gentleness and says, 'Yes, Lord; but I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred.'
