See how many things came together at once and laid siege to the man: illness, poverty, and the lack of anyone to stand up for him. 'While I am coming, someone else goes down ahead of me.' This is the most pitiable thing of all, enough to move even a stone. I seem to see the man crawling there every year, reaching the very mouth of the pool, and at the very last moment hanging on good hope, year after year. And what is greater still, [?] [Reg.: of the paralytic] [?] …say such things, the bed, carried aloft, becomes the accuser of their shamelessness. There is something

a third thing to say as well, no less important than what has been said. He ordered him to carry his bed so that you may learn that it was not human skill but divine power that did it all. In this way he gave the greatest and clearest proof of true and genuine health, so that none of those blasphemers could say that the paralytic was playing a part along with Christ and, as a favour to him, only pretended to walk. That is why he tells him to carry a load on his shoulders. If his limbs had not been firmly set and his joints made tight, he could not have carried such a bulk on his shoulders. Besides all this, something else was shown too: when Christ commands, everything happens at once, both release from disease and the return of health. Physicians may free people from their diseases, but they cannot bring the patient back to health at the same moment. They need another long stretch of time, for convalescence, to scrape away the remnants of the illness from the body little by little and drive them out. Not so with Christ. In a single instant he freed the man from his illness and restored his health, with no interval between. As soon as that sacred voice sprang from the holy tongue, the disease fled the body, the word became deed, and the whole illness was healed on every side. A rebellious maidservant, when she sees her own master, shrinks back and returns to proper order. In the same way the nature of the body, like a maidservant who had rebelled and brought on the paralysis, saw its own Master arrive, returned to its proper order and took up its fitting arrangement again. And the voice did all this, for these were not mere words but the words of God, of which Scripture says, 'Mighty are the works of his words.' If he made man when man did not exist, much more could he restore him when he had decayed and fallen apart. Here I would gladly ask those who pry into the essence of God: how did those limbs come together? How were the bones made tight? How was the slackened tone of the belly strengthened? How were the loosened sinews drawn taut again, and the strength that had been laid low raised up and set upright? They could not tell how. So simply marvel at what happened, and do not pry into the manner. When he had done as he was told and taken up his bed, the Jews saw him and said, 'It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to carry your mat on the Sabbath.' They ought to have worshipped the one who did it and marvelled at what had happened, but instead they argue about the Sabbath, truly straining out the gnat and swallowing the camel. What does the man say? 'The one who made me well said to me, "Take up your mat and walk."' Do you see the man's gratitude? He acknowledges his physician and declares that the one who gave the command deserves to be trusted. And just as the blind man reasoned with them,

…he offered proof that could not be disputed, and what he said, he demonstrated through his body. After this Jesus finds him and says to him, 'See, you have been made well. Sin no more, so that nothing worse happens to you.' Do you see the physician's wisdom? Do you see his care? He not only freed him from his present disease but also protects him for the future, and at just the right moment. While the man lay on his bed, Jesus said nothing of the kind and did not remind him of his sins, for the soul of the sick is somehow hard to please and miserable. But once he had driven away the illness and restored him to health, once he had given proof in deed of his power and his care, then he offers his counsel and exhortation at the right time, now shown to be trustworthy by his deeds themselves. Why, then, did the man go away and make him known to the Jews? Because he wanted them to share in the true teaching. But for this very reason, it says, they hated him and persecuted him. Pay attention to me here, for the whole contest lies here. 'This was why they persecuted him, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.' Let us see, then, how he defends himself. The way he makes his defence shows us whether he belongs among subjects or among the free, among those who serve or among those who command. What had happened seemed the greatest breach of the law. Once, after all, a man who gathered wood on the Sabbath was stoned for it, because he carried loads on the Sabbath. This was the great sin Christ was charged with: that he had broken the Sabbath. Let us see, then, whether he first asks for pardon like a slave and a subordinate, or whether he shows that he has power and authority, as the Master who presides over the law and himself gave the commandments. How does he defend himself? He says, 'My Father is working until now, and I am working.' Do you see his authority? If he were inferior to the Father and less than him, these words would be no defence at all, but a greater charge and a heavier accusation. Suppose someone does what only his superior is permitted to do, is caught and charged, and then says, 'Because my superior did it, I did it too.' This way of defending himself not only fails to clear him of the charges; it makes him liable to greater blame and accusation. It is arrogance and boastfulness to take on things above one's rank. So with Christ: if he were inferior, his words would be no defence but a greater charge. But since he was equal to the Father, there is no charge. If you like, I will make my point clear with an example. Only the king may wear purple and have a diadem on his head, and no one else. Now suppose some ordinary person is seen wearing this attire, is dragged into court and says, 'Because the king wears this attire, I wear it too.' He does not free himself from the accusation; by the way he defends himself he makes himself liable to a greater punishment and penalty. Again, to release the most shameful [?] [Reg.: of the same authority] [?]

…passes away, dissolves and perishes. Christ wanted to show that he belongs among those who provide and not those who are provided for, among those who act and not those who are acted upon. So he said, 'My Father is working, and I am working,' wanting to show that he stands equal with the Father. 5. Remember these things and keep them with all care. Weave together the wisdom of right living with soundness of doctrine. I urged this before, I urge it now, and I will not stop urging it. Nothing produces right living and wisdom as much as the time spent here. Land left untilled, with no one to water it, is full of thorns and thistles, while land that enjoys a farmer's hands flourishes, grows lush and teems with fruit. So too with the soul. The soul that enjoys the watering of the divine Scriptures flourishes, grows lush and teems with the fruit of the Spirit. But the soul left in drought and neglect, lacking such watering, becomes a wilderness, runs wild with growth and bears many thorns, which are the nature of sin. And where there are thorns, there are serpents, snakes, scorpions and all the power of the devil. If you do not believe what I say, come, let us compare those who stayed away with ourselves, and you will see how great the difference is. Better still, let us examine ourselves: at which times we are enjoying divine teaching, and at which times we have been cut off from this benefit for longer. Let us not, then, throw away so great a gain. The time spent here is the foundation of every good thing.
